speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-85, an Act to establish a corporation called Canagrex to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agricultural and food products from Canada, be read the third time and do
pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak at third reading of Bill C-85, legislation which will establish the Canadian agricultural export corporation, Canagrex. Long awaited, Canagrex will assist in the expansion of agriculture exports, particularly in the non-grain sector where in the past number of years we have experienced about a $2 billion trade deficit. Canagrex will be a catalyst to assist growth in export areas long considered the domain of some of other trading partners around the world and we will compete in a progressive-excuse the word-
Don't apologize.
-and positive action, using all the tools that Bill C-85 provides. Canagrex will not-
Will not be around long.

-and I want to repeat and emphasize this point-compete with Canadians. Canagrex will, however, within the context of the legislation, create an atmosphere for competitive growth on the export markets of the world for those products we have already identified as being "soft" in our over-all trade picture.
I am very disturbed over the statements made by the Official Opposition over the past few months, and again during report stage in the House last week. Still seemingly bent on creating a "bogeyman" out of this important piece of legislation, the Official Opposition has falsely claimed that Canagrex is a move by the Government to take over the agri-food industry.
Tying its argument into its stance on Crown corporations, the Official Opposition claims we do not need another Crown corporation and that through establishment of Canagrex the free enterprise attitudes within the agri-food industry will disappear. In one breath the Official Opposition says a loud
"No" to Canagrex based on its Crown corporation argument, and in the next breath the Official Opposition says you can have your Crown corporation, Mr. Minister or farmers of Canada, just so long as you remove the buy and sell powers contained in the Bill.
What are the Tories against, Mr. Speaker, Crown corporations?
That is a good question!

Is the Official Opposition really against Crown corporations? I do not really think so when you study the history of the Tory Party. My heavens, it was the Tories who began some of the most distinguished Crown corporations in this country.
Absolutely right.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was started by the Conservatives. The Canadian Wheat Board was started by the Conservatives and the Canadian National Railways was started by the Conservatives. The other day I heard one of the Members on the other side say: "Look at what the CN Railway has done". But he did not say: "We created it and we are sorry or we apologize for it", or anything else. He did not say that at all.
This is your last one. Go ahead.

No, the Tories are not against Crown corporations. They are against farmers in this country having the opportunity to become active players in the export game. What they are saying is that those farmers have no business in the export market. Even if they want to, they say: "We would like to deny you that right". Then they claim they are the friends of the farmers. I am surprised. I even know some of the Hon. Members' in-laws who are not of the same political faith that I am but are strong supporters of Canagrex, and they have told me what they have told their relations. Some Tories are only interested-and I am not putting them all in the same boat, but I know what some of them have told me privately-in maintaining the status quo when it comes to agri-food export development.
It is clear to me that the Tories are only interested in serving a specific sector of the agri-food industry when they request still further amendments on the buy-sell clause.
I have said many times in the past number of months, when the all-Party standing committee concluded its hearings on Bill C-85, there was consensus on the 14 amendments, and the

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
Tory Party's own agricultural critic, the former Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), who was on that committee, called the amendments reasonable. His words are recorded and he is a very reasonable person, of course. He realized the value of what the Bill would do, and he knows every effort was made by all Members of that committee to ensure Bill C-85 was equitable to all concerned.
He was particularly pleased to see us include the "at the request of' clause in the buy-sell portion of the Bill, and he expressed at the time that he felt it was something he could sell to his caucus. Being a reasonable person himself he figured the majority of the Conservative caucus feel the same way. Well, it appears he was not listened to, and if the Official Opposition had its way, farmers in this country would continue to lose valuable export opportunities and be made to sit on the fence.
I would point out, however, that Canadian farmers have never lost any freedom because of Crown corporations which operate under the authority of my Ministry.
That is absolutely ridiculous.

Mr. Speaker, I would challenge the Hon. Member to find examples of when any one of those Crown corporations was used other than to help farmers. In turn, by helping agriculture and farmers it helps the total society.
Let me refer to a few examples. There is the protection offered by the Farm Credit Corporation. All of them are asking me to expand the Farm Credit Corporation to take care of long-term farm loans and mortgages which are needed because the private sector is not properly looking after farm credit in the country. Also we have the Agricultural Stabilization Board, the Canadian Dairy Commission and prairie farm rehabilitation. Farmers are free to develop their farms under these organizations, choose their crops, improve their efficiency and become the most productive farmers in the world.
I challenge anyone to find anything that this Minister or this Government has done which has taken away any rights from the farmers of the land. We have given the farmers of the land more rights than in any other land in the entire world. Let that be a known fact.
And more problems.

The farmers in the United States of America do not have the same rights as our farmers. The farmers in Britain do not have the same rights as farmers here. The farmers in France do not have the same rights. The farmers in the U.S.S.R. do not have the same rights. The farmers in Poland to not have the same rights as those here. They hardly have any rights at all there. We are saying that it they want those rights they can have those rights. There is nothing "back door" about Crown corporations. They were established by Acts of Parliament and they report to Parliament, the ones for
which I am responsible. No one can accuse me of bringing in Canagrex through the back door.
You are responsible for closure.
Canagrex could have been brought in by Order in Council, if I had wanted to do it. 1 chose the legislative route.
What is the difference when you bring in closure?
I am very happy about having chosen the legislative route.
Are you happy about closure?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Minister of Agriculture has the floor.

No other piece of legislation in which I have ever been involved has had as much discussion as this since I have been Minister of Agriculture. It was before the Committee, before the House, before the Senate Committee on Agriculture. I have never seen that much discussion on any other piece of legislation with which I have had anything to do.
The Act to establish the agricultural export corporation is what is before the House. Hon. Members opposite continually point out bad things about Crown corporations. They hardly ever point out what the Auditor General said about this legislation. He said in his annual report: "I am happy to see that this Crown corporation will be the first". Afterwards when I asked him why he said that, he said it was because it was the first the Auditor General could go in and review completely at any time. He said: "Mr. Whelan, it is not only a first in Canada for the federal Government but it is a first for the Provinces. There is no other free country in the world which allows that of the Auditor General and what you are going to do with Canagrex to protect the public interest". How often do they report that; how often do they say that?
Then there was an amendment brought in by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), an NDP Member. He made a suggestion which the committee and I accepted. When they talk about the powers to buy and sell, other Provinces with Crown corporations have the power to buy and sell. For instance, in Alberta they have the power to buy and sell. They said that they could not even operate with their cattle sales agency if they did not have the power to buy and sell.
They did not bring it in by closure in Alberta.
Certainly not this Minister-
Oh, oh!
Did you ever hear of free speech?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The Minister of Agriculture has the floor.
June 13, 1983

No one on this side of the House, not this Minister of Agriculture, wants to set up any Crown corporation which is not answerable.
The Auditor General investigated the Canadian Dairy Commission. I asked him to do that. I had to ask him to do that because he does not have the authority to do it unless the Minister asks him. I asked him to review the operations of the Canadian Dairy Commission. He found some fault with it. I challenge anyone on either side of the House to point to any private corporation or Crown corporation and say that it is perfect. No such thing exists, as far as that goes. Even as well as I run the ones for which I am responsible, I would not say that they are perfect because I am not perfect myself.
It is a cop-out for Members opposite to accuse Crown corporations of fostering socialism and to suggest that same kind of philosophical free enterprise will solve all our problems. That kind of enterprise has been nothing more than philosophical for generations. Members opposite know that as well as anyone. Otherwise Alberta would be served by a private telephone company instead of a public one, Ontario residents would buy their liquor from private dealers instead of a Government-owned liquor control board operated store, and Quebec residents would buy their electricity from private power companies instead of Hydro-Quebec.
Crown corporations have been set up to deal with special needs. Why do we not recognize that? All Governments in Canada have recognized that special needs exist and that they have a responsibility as the elected representatives of the people to see that those needs are met. That is what we are doing here. Sometimes Governments have been able to provide assistance to private industry to meet the need. Where that has not been possible, the Crown corporation has proved to be an ideal way to solve the problem.
Setting up Government agencies to meet the public needs that are not being served by the private sector is not unique to Canada. Nearly every Government in the world does that; yes, even the great free enterprise Government to the south of us in the United States of America does that. Check what it has done.
They don't bring in closure.
They do not have to bring in closure because they have a more responsible House, with rules under which you cannot do the same things that can be done here. We never brought in closure.
You brought in closure.

The Member keeps using the word "closure". We brought in time allocation. Closure means just what it says-bang, closed, a one-day debate, a vote by 1 a.m. the next morning. Time allocation in the Mother of Parliaments under Her Majesty is used almost every day. They have a business committee of the House. They do that in a gentlemanly way.
Canagrex
If there is anything unique about Canada's Crown corporations, it is their effectiveness in carrying out their responsibilities and their accountability to Parliament. We have a proud record. Let us look at some that we have right here in this capital. Anyone who looks down the list of Crown corporations and evaluates what they have done will have to admit their effectiveness.
There is a Crown corporation which handles museums in this country. Look at the magnificent job the National Capital Commission has done in developing Ottawa, Hull and the surrounding area. The National Research Council has a worldwide reputation. You must also look at the role of the Canada Council in promoting the arts. These corporations are outside of my territory a bit, but I am well aware of them, as are Members opposite. Would they want to destroy those Crown corporations? They have the power to buy and sell the National Capital Commission. In a farm magazine I read this morning, it stated that the ploughing match will be held in this area in late September. The article brags about the green belt which the National Capital Commission has preserved around this city. That has been tremendous for this city. It is a Crown corporation which kept this belt around the city. Would Members opposite have the nerve to say to the Members of Parliament from the national capital area that they want to abolish the National Capital Commission and set up something different? I would dare them to do that.
Canagrex will enable Canada for the first time to deliver a co-ordinated approach to export marketing in this country, something that we have never had. It will provide new opportunities for exporters, the traditional trader as well as the newcomers to the export market field. What all of this means is increased dollar gains on international markets for Canada and increased job opportunities at home. Regardless of what anyone says, it means jobs. Under our agri-food strategy, we can see that in the next 15 years we will be providing 150,000 to 200,000 new jobs.
I believe that one of the most exciting aspects of the Canagrex legislation is that it will facilitate the entry of new exporters, thereby allowing for greater diversity of Canadian agri-food products on the export market. Through the creation of Canagrex, doors will open to potential exporters, big and small, which for many years have remained closed. Canada's potential in agri-food export marketing, while not unlimited, certainly has not been tapped to its fullest. We have the resources in the country to enable us really to begin to do a job in an area once considered too tough to conquer. It is a matter of knowing what our true potential really is and then setting our goals and coming up with an effort that is tough for the competition to beat.
I find it simply amazing that there is still concern that the federal Government is creating an agent that will take over the entire agri-food industry. Nothing could be further from the truth, and I repeat nothing, and one only needs to read the

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
legislation to realize that that is not the intent of the legislation, Mr. Speaker. Its express purpose is to assist export expansion and nothing more. Canagrex will act as a facilitator to the agricultural export industry.
Some may be surprised by the people who are ready for this legislation and want to work with it.
Then why do you have to use closure?

We are not trying to take business away from the private trade, as some have suggested. We want private enterprise to grow and to continue to play its historical and important role in the development of Canada's export trade. If the remainder of our exports are compared with our total imports, it can be seen that there was a non-grain agricultural trade deficit of about $2 billion. Canada has the resources to do much better than that, Mr. Speaker.
The key to generating increased agri-food production is to improve market development and Canagrex will play a vital part in that development. Nowhere is Canagrex given monopoly power over any commodity. Its powers can only be used in conjunction with private trade to facilitate export. It cannot be involved, as was said here the other day, in putting little cans that say "Canagrex" on the walls of the supermarkets in Canada. Any person with common sense who reads the legislation can see that it is that plain. The amendments have been made in a way that will not allow that to happen.
Cries of a takeover conspiracy by the opponents to Bill C-85 are the most absurd cries I have ever heard.
You deny us a right even to speak on it.

Those opponents are selfishly trying to destruct an export mechanism that the majority of the industry has requested for years.
Members of the Official Opposition know that they have not fairly addressed a recognized problem when they criticize this legislation. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, with its membership of over 200,000 Canadian farmers, want this Bill. It is a producers' Bill and producers have every right to be players in the agricultural export world. To deny them that right is undemocratic because Canadian farmers rely heavily on exports. They rely on exports more than any other group of farmers in the world.
Canadian farmers do not want it.

Upwards of 50 per cent of Canadian farmers' income comes from export while approximately 30 per cent of American farmers' income comes from export. It can be seen how important export is to farmers in the country. It can be understood why such a healthy agricultural industry has been built over a period of time within our cold, northern hemisphere climate. At one time the geographical location of Canada led many people to say that it would be impossible to develop an agricultural industry in the country. We have developed one, Mr. speaker, that is the envy of the world. Studies have shown that while as a nation we have taken positive steps in agricultural export trading over the years, there is still a need to diversify the commodities we offer on
world markets. For this reason, and as a means of focusing attention on the Canadian agricultural trade effort, the Canagrex legislation is timely.
When reading Bill C-85, it can be clearly seen that Can-garex's powers to buy and sell can only be exercised in relation to its purposes, which are to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agricultural products subject to the following limitations: Canagrex can only engage in the export of agricultural products when invited to enter into ventures jointly or in co-operation with, or at the request of, Canadian companies, co-operatives, marketing boards, associations, individuals carrying on business in Canada or contracts with foreign Governments.
Second, the power to purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold real property for actual use by Canagrex in the operation and management of its business does not, Mr. Speaker-and I must repeat, does not-include power to purchase, lease or otherwise acquire real property for the production of fruit, forage, grain, vegetables or other crops, the raising of cattle, poultry, sheep, swine or other livestock or the processing of any agricultural or food product. Those limitations are as clear as a bell.
Those amendments were made and the Hon. Member for Elgin said that they were reasonable. He said: "The Minister has been more flexible than I expected him to be". This is on the record. Moreover, on the criticism of Canagrex's power to enter into joint ventures with the private trade and the farm organizations-
You know not what you do.
You can see how democratic the Opposition is being, Mr. Speaker.
We did not bring in closure. You brought in closure, not us.

We brought in time allocation. Every democratic Parliament in the world accepts time allocation. It is a good thing to deal with legislation. Hon. Members opposite want a form of anarchy.
I should like to note that a number of provincial Crown corporations, such as those in Saskatchewan, Quebec and Prince Edward Island, already have the power to buy and sell. In Alberta they have the power to buy and sell, to purchase property and do whatever they want.
They don't bring it in by closure.

The federal Government, under the Agricultural Products Board Act has had the power to buy and sell since 1952. I would challenge any Member in the House to find out when this Act was used by any Minister of any political stripe to harm agriculture. It has always been used to assist agriculture. We are using it in Ontario at the present time to buy up tomatoes and surplus canned products. We are putting $8 million into that program. We are using it in British
June 13, 1983

Columbia and have used it practically every Province in Canada-but at their request. It was at the request of the Canadian food processors of this country that we used that power.
But you have to be Liberal to get it.

The federal Government has had these powers.
1 would challenge the Hon. Member to find any Conservative Minister who has abused the powers vested in him to administer the Agricultural Products Board Act. It has never been abused. It has never been used to hurt but always to help. Hon. Members opposite should study a little history.
What about the national energy policy? It is just a boondoggle.

The power to buy and sell is in keeping with standard business practices. A necessary tool of Canagrex is properly to serve the agricultural export industry.
As a point of information, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to what Mr. Tony Saretsky of the Alberta Canada All Breeds Association said when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture on May 12, 1982. Responding to a Committee member, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), Mr. Saretsky said his association had the power to buy and sell. Imagine that, in Alberta, Mr. Speaker. He said he could not operate if he did not have the authority to buy and sell, that he could not work until he got that authority. Is the power to buy and sell called free enterprise when it is in Alberta and when the federal Government gives the authority to join together to buy and sell to all the Provinces that do not have the resources that Alberta has, is that socialism? Is it free enterprise when it is provincial? I do not understand that philosophy and I do not think anyone else does Mr. Speaker.
As was pointed out during that stage, what was most interesting was the fact that Mr. Saretsky indicated to the Committee that originally his association did not have the power to buy and sell. The full text of his statement may be found on page 28, Issue 67 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
1 might add, Mr. Speaker, that the power to buy and sell under the Canagrex legislation is not going to be directed at traditional export traders of agricultural products in this country. In fact, although Hon. Members doubt this, many Hon. Members and many farm leaders have said: "As long as Whelan remains Minister of Agriculture, we do not have to worry about the legislation." It is there to ensure that Canagrex will be able to respond to any situation which might arise.
No other Minister of Agriculture in Canada would bring in closure.

Canadian farmers see the wisdom of an agency that would tie together the export practices of the public and private sectors and strengthen our thrust into foreign markets. Other countries are doing it so why should the Canadian
Canagrex
agricultural industry not have the same kind of tools that other countries have to ensure that we do not lag behind?
It is interesting to note that while Canagrex was being discussed, developed, amended and politicized, the United States increased its capacity to deal on the export market through passage of the Export Trading Act. It never had to use time allocation because it saw the need, charged ahead and did it.
But the Members designed it, not the bureaucrats.

President Reagan signed the Act into law on October 8, 1982, giving the American agricultural industry yet another tool to help capture agri-food markets around the world. The purpose of the new law in the United States is to stimulate U.S. exports by facilitating export trading companies, export trade associations and more export trade services in general.
In Great Britain a couple of months ago, just before Mrs. Thatcher decided to call an election, they established a law called "Food From Britain" to establish a new marketing organization whose prime function will be to help co-ordinate and promote marketing initiatives throughout Britain and the world.
For those reasons and the fact that other countries such as Israel, France, Germany and Australia all have comprehensive export trading and promotional mechanisms, it is important for Canada to act.
I am pleased with and proud of this legislation, Mr. Speaker, because it is what the majority of farmers in this country asked for. I am pleased because producers have had a recognized need addressed positively with this legislation. They now have the needed tool to assist expansion of agri-food products.
I am also proud, Mr. Speaker, because I know of the long and dedicated hours so many people have given to the drafting of this Bill. One person I would particularly like to pay a compliment to is Dr. Dennis Ware who, while attending a conference in Europe on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, suffered a heart attack. Dr. Ware is a most dedicated civil servant and his team at Agri-food Canada unselfishly gave of their time and their talents to ensure that this legislation was written as equitably and as responsive as is humanly possible. I worked with Dr. Ware for months. Some of the other Hon. Members know him also. He is home in Ottawa now convalescing. There is no more dedicated person and no more serious and honest Canadian than this man, and he comes from western Canada, British Columbia. He saw the need because he understands the world situation. He was the person with whom we all worked. The former Minister of Agriculture on the other side of the House worked with him also, and he knows of what I speak.

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
What is currently paramount in agri-food trade application for Canada is that we do have the necessary facilitators in place to ensure Canada can do the best job possible, to work with, to assist, to facilitate. That is how Canada was built, not by-no, 1 will not say what I was thinking. Canagrex will be one of those facilitators, Mr. Speaker.
In a spirit of co-operation and exercising the greatest planning and care, I am very optimistic that Canadian agrifood export marketing has a bright future to look forward to. We know that by the respect we have built over a period of years around the world and by the relationship which our farmers have adopted with many, many different peoples around the world. Our farm organizations do not live under a little umbrella or under a basket. They recognize what is going on in the rest of the world. They are the ones who asked for this legislation. They are the ones who thought up this legislation. We promised this legislation in two election campaigns. It has been delayed in this House.
Mir. Taylor: They did not ask for closure.
I am not ashamed one bit to bring in time allocation.
You are proud of closure.

Time allocation is something which the Mother of Parliament uses practically every week, if not every day, in the House of Commons procedures in Great Britain. It recognizes that it is an important tool to make sure that Parliament works.
Parliament working under closure stops Parliament from working.

Some Hon. Members here have used the word "closure", and they continue to use the word "closure", which is not accurate, Mr. Speaker. It is dishonest as far as I am concerned. After some 85 hours of debate in committee and in the House, and after the Senate holding hearings for nearly half that many hours, to say we are putting in closure is false, false, false. When we say "time allocation", in essence, what we are saying is: "The people have asked for this. The majority of them want this. It is time we quit talking about it and put it into action."
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a question I would like to put to the Minister. I understand we ask questions. I have been in the House for about 11 years. During that time I have served continuously on the Agriculture Committee and I found it to be a very co-operative Committee, particularly in the earlier years. Hon. Member from all sides of the House were doing their utmost to do their best for agriculture. However, in the last two or three years, I have seen a certain stubbornness develop on the part of the Minister.
Where is the question?
He does not have to ask a question. He is making a comment.

The Minsiter had better read the rules, Mr. Speaker. I can make both comments and ask questions, and I am coming to my question. I said that in the last two or three years I have detected a certain stubbornness on the part of the Minister in refusing to co-operate with the members of the Agriculture Committee to do what is best in the interests of the producers of Canada.
During the Committee hearings we talked about the part which Industry, Trade and Commerce plays in our export trade. We talked about the part which people in External Affairs play throughout the world in exports. We asked to have representatives from those Departments brought to that Committee for the purpose of discussing with them the effectiveness of what they were doing, in order that we could determine whether or not we needed Canagrex, whether the power should go to IT&C or External Affairs, or whether IT&C and External Affairs power should come to Canagrex. Can the Minister tell the people of this country why he refused to allow witnesses from those two Departments to appear before the Committee in order to let the Committee have the full story so that they could make a decision as to what was best for the producers of this country?

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I do not have anything to say about the people from Industry, Trade and Commerce, External Affairs, or anyone else appearing before that committee. The Hon. Member cannot find anything in the records to show that I stopped them from coming before the Committee. He is putting something on the record here today which is just not fact. Those people are under another Ministry; they are not under the Ministry of Agriculture. This Bill is being sponsored by the Minister of Agriculture. The opportunity to question them about what they do is when that Ministry's estimates are before the committee responsible for hearing those estimates at that time.
When the Hon. Member says this Minister is stubborn, inflexible, refusing to co-operate, I ask you to consider this little Bill of 41 Sections, which has had 14 amendments, quite a few of which were put forward by the Opposition and accepted by us. The agriculture critic put those amendments before the Committee and we said they were good. The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) is disagreeing with his official agriculture critic because the records show what the Hon. Member for Elgin said at that time. He more or less acted surprised that I did accept the amendments and so on; he went that far. He said I was being quite reasonable and responsible. Yet the Hon. Member says I am being irresponsible and stubborn.
I was chairman of the Agriculture Committee, Mr. Speaker, when it had 45 members. I ask the Hon. Member to look back and see how well it was run when it had 45 members. It was a well run committee. We got along with Members from all the Parties. When I said to the other Parliaments of the world that we had 45 members on the Agriculture Committee, they said
June 13, 1983

it was unbelievable, how did I make it work? The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw did recognize it worked and that there was a feeling of co-operation and a desire to do things to help agriculture in this country.
The Hon. Member says I am responsible in the last three years for this feeling disappearing. I say to him he must share the responsibility because Hon. Members opposite are the ones who politicized Canagrex. When it was brought into the House, the official Leader of the Opposition, who can sit in the House at the present time-he was House Leader at that time-said; "We welcome this legislation because it was thought up by the Hon. Member for Elgin". I believe he said something like that; I may be a little inaccurate. I see the Hon. Member for Elgin just about ready to jump up on a point of order. However, he did say "We welcome this legislation", and the verbiage was something like "Because it was ours". The records are there, Mr. Speaker, for you to see. 1 am sure some of my colleagues will put on the record later word for word what was said. I believe the Hon. Member for Kent (Mr. Bossy) put on the record the interview of the Hon. Member for Elgin when he was Minister of Agriculture, or before he was Minister of Agriculture, talking about Canagrex, about what he was going to do with it and how he was going to make it work. It is all in the records, Mr. Speaker. But I am the one who is supposed to be stubborn?
I find it confusing, Mr. Speaker, to see Hon. Members opposite changing their minds. I find it confusing when I hear the Hon. Member still talking from the back benches over there, and that is probably where he will talk from for years and years, from the back bench. He refuses to recognize that in his own Province of Alberta they have Crown corporations which have the power to buy and sell.
We did not bring them in by closure.

The Hon. Member calls that free enterprise. They have a banking system. They have an airline system. They own half of the land and they own pretty near all of the resources. He calls that the free enterprise system. The most socialized Province in Canada is Alberta.
We did not bring them in by closure.

Saskatchewan is like a little bitty chicken alongside of Alberta, as far as that goes. When the Hon. Member talks about free enterprise, let him look in his own House. He was partly responsible for that at one time in Alberta, perhaps not for everything that they did when he was in the Government of Alberta, but 1 studied some of these things and he never once tried to squash, according to the records I have seen, a Crown corporation in Alberta. He never once tried to do that kind of thing.
We did not bring them in by closure.

He let them grow while he was in Alberta. The Minister of Agriculture of Alberta has a Crown corporation which can buy and sell.
Canagrex
On a point of order, the man is telling complete lies and he should know it.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Withdraw!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that he has used an unparliamentary term and I invite him to rephrase his remarks.
What the Member has been saying is completely untrue. Completely untrue and he knows it. He does not know a thing about Alberta when he calls it socialism.
I rise on a question of privilege, because the Hon. Member did not withdraw what he has said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has withdrawn his remarks.
No, he did not say he withdrew the remarks. He said it was completely untrue and I say what I said is true.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In the judgment of the Chair the Hon. Member has reconstructed his remarks in such a way as to be parliamentary.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House would agree we have just witnessed another spectacle of ministerial misunderstanding and misinterpretation, a great deal of ministerial political mischief, and indeed ministerial garbage. There is certainly no question about that.
If you check the record, Mr. Speaker, you will find that for the eighteenth time this session this Government is using closure to stop debate on vitally important legislation. The Minister refers to it as time allocation; that is nonsense. It is just a play on words. There is no difference between time allocation and closure. It is closure on legislation in the case of Canagrex, which could have-and I emphasize "could have"-profoundly detrimental effects on the future of the Canadian agriculture industry.
I cannot understand the Minister's logic in pushing through this legislation at this time. If he were serious about the need for this new Crown corporation, then why did he not push it through two days after he moved the closure motion on December 16? Is it because he feels opposition to the Bill has died down? That is certainly not the case. My colleagues and I continue to receive large numbers of letters and telegrams of protest which point out the weaknesses but, more importantly, the dangers of this Bill.
These problems were pointed out in the Standing Committee on Agriculture where some 20 out of the 32 groups appearing before it opposed the Bill, specifically its broad and ill-defined buy and sell powers. Agricultural groups like the Western Barley Growers said:
-excessive power given to Canagrex worries us as it may be used as a tool for income transfer to various areas of the country.

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
The Alberta Canola Growers Association testified:
Our organization disagrees with the need for a federal agency to act as a principal in the sale of agriculture products. We support an organization that has the role of an agent only.
The flax growers said of Canagrex's broad buy and sell powers that it-
-presents a serious threat to the continued existence of privately or cooperatively owned businesses engaged in marketing our products.
The Palliser Wheat Growers indicated that the greatest impediment to more aggressive production and marketing programs for most prairie farm products is excessive Government regulation. These regulations, together with the associated Government bureaucracy, bear down on agriculture and interfere with the development of a strong production and marketing thrust. They say that they have seen no evidence that the trade is not well able to do an effective marketing job with those Canadian products produced at competitive world prices if the legislative environment permits that trade to function and function normally. The Alberta All Breeds Association said:
The reality of Canagrex is that foreign Governments would have little incentive to transact business with anyone in Canada but Canagrex.
The Canadian Meat Council said:
Our main concern with the Canagrex proposal is that it will interfere and detract from the successful accomplishments and/or duplicate existing achievements.
The western stockgrowers say that Government should legislate so that it supports the private sector and should never attempt to suppress or stifle the initiative of the businessman and the entrepreneur. The Canadian Cattlemen's Association said:
We should walk before we run and not proceed with undue haste to create a structure that may be inappropriate to our needs. Canagrex may become a direct marketing agent in its own right and thus go far beyond the promotional, facilitating and support functions originally envisioned.
Let us travel to eastern Canada, I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) will be interested in what the Prince Edward Island Potato Marketing Board had to say about his colleague's Bill. They said:
We are in agreement with the purposes of the Bill in so far as promoting and facilitating the export of seed and tablestock potatoes are concerned, but we emphatically disagree with Government agency becoming engaged in the export of Prince Edward Island seed or tablestock potatoes if "becoming engaged" includes buy and sell.
I can remember, Mr. Speaker, some time ago when this Bill was front and centre during farm meetings as one travelled across the country, having the opportunity to be in Prince Edward Island and to meet with some of these people. They told me very emphatically that there was some misinterpretation and misunderstanding with reference to what was really meant by the term "engage in". I remember their making it very clear to me that if that meant to buy and sell, then certainly to count them out. Even those agricultural organizations which testified in favour of Canagrex were concerned about the buy and sell powers. The Canadian Pork Council said:
We believe that, unless the present marketing agencies are not responsive or not aggressive enough to apparent marketing opportunities, Canagrex should not be involved in commodity trading.
The Canadian Horticultural Council warned that any effort by Canagrex in international trade should not conflict with or work against the efforts presently underway by industry organizations. Even the Ontario Flue Cured Tobacco Marketing Board down in my part of the country, which has probably been one of the greatest supporters of the Canagrex legislation, testified that present exporters must be assured that the purpose of Canagrex is to assist, and that it will not in any way oppose or interfere with the present export activities being carried on by the Marketing Board. I challenge the Minister to stand here today and speak to that Board and the producers, as well as the Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board and the Soy Bean Marketing Board in our part of the country, and give them an iron-clad commitment that indeed Canagrex, given the power it has, will not interfere. I challenge him to do that but I know he cannot respond.
The buy and sell powers of the legislation are too broad and ill-defined. In committee we also heard not the Department of Agriculture advisers, Mr. Speaker, but indeed the Department of Justice legal advisers admit that the legislation was loose and there was no definite commitment on the part of Canagrex to co-operate with or indeed receive approval from commodity groups and marketing boards in the selling of their product. They warned us of that.
In other words, the broad buy and sell powers of Canagrex could-and this is important to the producers and farmers in Ontario-if misused, usurp the powers of the provincial commodity marketing boards. Because Canagrex would want to be part of as many lucrative export deals as possible in order to be successful, which is a natural assumption, our traditional agricultural exporters could be cut off from marketing information available to their agents by Canagrex and other Government departments and agencies.
The Government brought forward an amendment in committee which would restrict Canagrex to buy and sell only in joint ventures and upon request. However, this restriction was then swept aside with the admission that a joint venture could be made with as few as one individual.
The Minister has stated that Canagrex would be a valuable tool to shore up Canadian commodity prices in the export market. However, the commodity prices would be forced down instead of up if Canagrex contracts were opened up for bidding. If they were not opened up for bidding, obviously one area of the country could be played off against the other. While I am not saying this would necessarily happen, there is that risk. As far as we are concerned, that risk cannot be taken.
I will not follow the Minister's example of taking everything that I hear and see as gospel truth, but in my travels across the country I have been told that the Minister has indicated that it would help to increase export prices because it could indeed be
June 13, 1983

subsidized. I do not believe the Minister even said that and he is shaking his head negatively. Eiowever that feeling is obviously out there across the country and has surfaced at at least a dozen meetings at which 1 have taken questions from the floor seeking to clarify this matter. It should definitely be clarified that Canagrex, even given the sweeping powers that it now has, does not have the power to subsidize a Canadian agricultural product in the export market.
The Minister has also said that Canagrex would only use its buy and sell powers in unusual or extraordinary circumstances. But the Minister already has these powers and spoke about them earlier this morning. I refer to the powers of the Agricultural Products Board. My colleagues and 1 believe that by having to go to Cabinet according to the terms of the Agricultural Products Board Act, that would certainly give some type of protection with reference to the business that could be transacted by the corporation.
The only protection presently offered to those organizations fearful of Canagrex' broad buy and sell powers is the Minister's word. While I can only speak for myself, a Minister's word is pretty small comfort to me. The Minister's word that the powers would only be used in unusual circumstances is not good enough for me. I am sure that it is not good enough for the majority of Canadian farmers in this country.
During his career, which is about to come to an end, the Minister has made many, many promises. Can the House remember the promises about cheap money for farmers? Does it remember the promises about the agri-bond concept? Does it remember the promise about capital gains legislation? Does it remember the promise about a stabilization program for beef farmers in this country? The list goes on and on. However, I want to deal specifically with this Bill and utilize my time to speak on behalf of the Canadian farmers, for whom the Minister indicated, very inappropriately and inaccurately, that we did not speak.
Canadian agriculture deserves more protection than the Minister's word. Our amendments to Clause 14 and related clauses of the Bill would have provided the protection that the Canadian agri-food industry needs. The Minister has discounted our concerns and the concerns of many farm groups across the country. He said that the adoption of four or five amendments by the committee should ease our concern. Certainly we appreciate the amendments that were accepted by the Government, but these were technical amendments, in essence, and not very substantive. One amendment dealt with a language change and he had no option but to accept our other amendment because it was simply a reminder that the amendment was necessary to make Canagrex compatible with Crown corporation legislation.
Let there be no doubt that the intent of our more substantive amendments dealt specifically with the removal of powers to buy and sell and engage in joint ventures. That is the thrust of our amendments and it is unfortunate that it required about 14 or 15 amendments. We cannot be blamed for that because we did not write the Bill. The Minister's advisers wrote the Bill and in our response to make certain that these powers were
Canagrex
removed it was necessary for us not simply to introduce one amendment to Clause 14 but to introduce a number.
Despite the Minister's promises, Canagrex could become a power unto itself. The Auditor General does not offer sufficient protection against abuses by Canagrex. He only reports on the financial accountability of Crown corporations. He does not examine whether politics interfere or have influence on commercial dealings and decisions. As well, his reports can be ignored. For example, his report questioned the benefit to the Canadian taxpayers of Petro-Canada's purchase of Petrofina, and his inability to get sufficient information from Petro-Canada gives us some idea of the shortcomings of the powers of the Auditor General and his Department.
The need for Parliament to approve Canagrex' budget does not offer sufficient protection either. Parliament can certainly ask questions about it, but bearing in mind majority Governments, these budgets always receive approval in the end.
As well, the ability of Parliament to review corporate plans does not offer sufficient protection. Canadair had a corporate plan and it cost the Canadian taxpayer some $1.5 billion. The five-year review also does not offer sufficient protection against Canagrex abuses. The review is simply that; it is a parliamentary review. It is not a sunset clause. I know that my colleague from Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) had very vigorously pursued the opportunity to implement a real sunset clause. Of course, it was denied.
Some farm groups have urged that the board of directors of Canagrex include a majority of producers in order to protect their interests. However, there is nothing in the Bill which requires this. Instead, the board will be appointed at the discretion of Cabinet and it would therefore not be too surprising to think that political contracts rather than agricultural knowledge would be involved in the selection.
In this respect it is rather interesting to recall that the Minister is always standing in the House and on public platforms across the country saying that various organizations support him. He says that a majority of producers support him. That is nonsense. He is inaccurate. I have heard him stand in the House on a number of occasions to say that he has the complete support of the largest farm organization in Canada, meaning the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. That is not absolutely true. The fact is that the position of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is that they are supportive of this legislation but they place a condition upon it. That condition is that the majority of the people on the board of directors be producers. Again, the Minister of Agriculture cannot stand in the House and give us that commitment. When it comes to the bottom line, he obviously does not have the complete and full support of the largest farm organization in the country, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I am sure that the greatest disservice the Minister has imposed on the Canadian agricultural industry could be Canagrex. In the first clause of the Bill he has imposed the unpopular and potentially disastrous buy and sell powers. It is my opinion and indeed that of those farm organizations which particularly have had some considerable experience in the

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
export of agricultural products in the export market that the most important part of the Bill is the need for export credits and insurance. That is what the Canadian agricultural industry needs. That is what the Canadian agricultural organizations need. They do not need the buy and sell powers; they need export credits and export insurance. That is the guts of the Bill.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude by saying that the buy and sell powers are not needed. The agricultural groups did not urge and have not been urging-those people have been somewhat supportive-the passage of this Bill because of the buy and sell powers, not at all. They have been urging the support of this Bill on the basis of the need for export credits and insurance.
The Minister has said that the Canadian agricultural exporters have not been doing an effective job. He has claimed they have missed too many opportunities. I am going to be very honest with you, Mr. Speaker. I had some mixed feelings about the job that some of our Canadian exporters were doing; but after having provided them an opportunity to come before the committee and to hear some of the evidence and to see some of the results of some of the private exporters and some of the agricultural organizations, particularly those in western Canada, I certainly had no doubts in my mind, when I saw the results, that many of the private organizations were doing an excellent job. They could have been doing a better job, I am sure, if they had been provided the export credits and the export insurance. That is what is needed.
We do not need a Government buying and selling through a Crown corporation. We do not need this Government agency interfering with the marketplace. The Liberal Government has abundantly and clearly shown in the oil industry that it is not able to do better than, or even do a comparable job to, the private sector; yet the Minister refused to consider these arguments. They were made by all members on the committee. They were made by the majority of farm organizations which appeared before the committee.
What is the purpose of bringing witnesses before the standing committee? In my opinion and in our Party's opinion, I am certain the purpose is to talk to the people working in this specific area day in and day out. Those are the people who really know what is going on, not the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) or the agricultural critic. The committee provides an excellent opportunity to get up-to-date, accurate information on what is going on in the international field. We have done that. We got the message loud and clear; there is no question about that at all. The message almost without exception was that we did not need the buy and sell powers in Canagrex.
I stand to be corrected because this was a long time ago, but 1 do recall that the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, if they had had a choice, probably would have opted not to have this legislation at all. The second organization-and the Minister
brags and boasts about having the largest organization supporting this Bill, which is nonsense and garbage-is the Consumers Association of Canada. That is the largest lobby organization there is in this country. The Consumers Association represents 300,000 farmers and 24 million people. That was the largest organization which made a presentation to us in committee. This organization would have preferred to have Canagrex killed and not to have surfaced at all.
What did the Minister do? He completely ignored this accurate, up-to-date information. Instead he launched and spent several thousand dollars in the preparation of a publication called "Canagrex-Responding to the Need". He tried to make the claim that he speaks on behalf of Canadian agriculture. That is absolute nonsense. He has completely ignored the input we received in committee. We did not ignore it. We got the message loud and clear. I had some doubts about how effective this corporation could be. There is no question that it is going to become a reality. The Liberals have a majority and they can do what they want.
And the Minister is.

And the Minister is doing what he wants, as my colleague from Provencher (Mr. Epp) accurately responds. We got the message. People do not want the powers of buy and sell.
Let me get back to Canagrex responding to the need. This is another example of wasteful Liberal Government spending, the spending of several thousands of dollars of taxpayers' money. In the eyes of this publication Canagrex has no problems. It is that little piece of legislation containing some 40 pages. Canagrex is equated with the salvation of agricultural products exporters. Just talk to the agricultural products exporters and see if they look upon Canagrex as being the salvation of their industry, Mr. Speaker. It even contains two-probably the only two-editorials which have appeared in support of Canagrex. I questioned the Minister through Order Paper Question No. 4,529 as to why the publication did not include any of the more than 20 editorials which had appeared at that time condemning Canagrex. The Minister responded that such editorials could not be found. He responded that none could be found.
I question the accuracy of that response. If this marks the level of his research-and I have a higher regard for his research than that-then I can understand why his cabinet colleagues do not take him seriously and why they have tried to suppress many of his initiatives.
In order to help the Minister, I would like to point out to him some of the editorials which, indeed, have been missed. Does the Minister or his officials not monitor the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix! It covers a wide agricultural area. On June 8, 1982, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix in an editorial wrote:
Given the breadth of opposition it's difficult to imagine who, outside of Whelan and his bureaucrats, supports the proposal.
There, Mr. Minister, is an editorial that appeared in the Star-Phoenix June 8, 1982. It is interesting to note that on
June 13, 1983

July 6, 1982 someone by the name of Eugene Whelan wrote a response to this editorial indicating it was wrong.
Eugene who?
Eugene Whelan.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Who is he?
The Minister should be concerned about someone using his name since this is one of the editorials which he claimed he had not found.

Oh, oh!
In an editorial in the Edmonton Journal on June 4, 1982, we read:
Given the current mistrust of state management, and of the long term plans of Ottawa bureaucrats, perhaps the correct response is to confine Canagrex to export promotion. It should prove itself capable of walking before it runs.
I could not agree more with that editorial from the Edmonton Journal.
Did Eugene Whelan write that?

I do not think the Minister wrote that editorial, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister could have missed those editorials written in the larger urban newspaper, but surely the Minister would have read the editorial of May, 1982 that appeared in the Country Guide. It reads:
Once again Eugene Whelan has been unable to distinguish between the important and the totally insignificant. After 10 years the farm community has become accustomed to this, one can but hope, however, that cooler heads prevail and Canagrex is killed before it multiplies.
Hear, hear!

I am sure the Minister would not have missed the editorial in Agriweek which appeared in May, 1983. It reads:
Mr. Whelan's eagerness to establish still another bureaucracy has outdistanced any effort to diagnose the real cause of our sputtering food exports. As a result, he has developed a sizeable multi-faceted organization without first defining precisely the problems to be solved. In his zeal to do something, Mr. Whelan has devised a plan based on good intentions and motherhood statements and one that reveals an astounding lack of rigorous thinking.
In the July editorial that appeared in Food Canada last year, it was indicated that Bill C-85 was too loosely written and too open-ended. Also it indicated that the restraints on such a federal corporation, if it must exist, should be spelled out in clear terms; otherwise Canagrex could indeed become "Canagarbage".
These are only a few editorials that appeared prior to the end of August, 1982, the date of the last editorial in the publication "Canagrex responding to the need". I am not surprised they were not included in the publication. However, I am amazed that the Minister would have the arrogance to say that he never saw any of the opposing editorials. Has he seen or read any of the more than 100 editorials and articles which condemned Canagrex? I am sure he has. If not, I would be
Canagrex
very happy to send the Minister copies of them. I think it is important to indicate that even papers which originally-
Some editorial writers do not know anything about agriculture.

The Minister says that some papers do not know anything about agriculture. I would disagree, but I would also be inclined to agree that many of them do, and a lot of them come from large urban areas. I would not like to make the statement the Minister made, that most farm papers do not know much about agriculture.
I said "editorial writers".

Even papers which originally endorsed Canagrex have had second thoughts. Not only newspapers and farm papers but many farmers and farm organizations, not knowing much about it, were originally impressed with the efforts of the Government to establish a greater priority in the export of agricultural products. Everybody supports that. We support that. There is no question about that. There are many ways in which this can be done. Many farmers and their organizations support the facilitating aspect of Canagrex. My Party and I support that, there is no question about it. Many farmers and agricultural organizations support the need for export credits and export insurance.
There is no question about the fact that there is such a need out there. I support that, we support that, but it comes down to the bottom line. Some of us have doubts about the buy and sell powers. There is no question about that either. After going through committee and obtaining the information and the feelings of individuals in farm organizations, there should be no question about the message out there. They support the things about which I talked earlier. There is no question about the fact that they do not support it, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which placed a condition on it. Even farm papers which originally endorsed Canagrex have had second thoughts. There is a prime example. Originally Farm and Country endorsed Canagrex, although it recommended that it should be subject to a sunset clause or a sunset law. That was the position of Farm and Country at the beginning of this debate. In the interval they have had an opportunity, the same opportunity as my colleagues and I and the same opportunity as the Minister and his colleagues, to hear credible witnesses, people who are in the business, make their pitch and presentation. There should be no question about that whatsoever. Any thinking person, any person with respect for information supplied by people who know what they are talking about, should take the same position we have or the same position which Farm and Country took on January 18, 1983, at which time its editorial called upon the Minister to compromise on the buy and sell powers. After having an opportunity to look at the Bill, Farm and Country indicated that the Minister should compromise on the buy and sell powers.
Another excellent recommendation in that editorial was the suggestion that these powers should be hoisted for five years so that Canagrex could prove its worth as a promoter and

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
facilitator. If it could prove its worth, if it could be demonstrated at the time of the parliamentary review that it needed the power to buy and sell, we would have been in a very difficult position to deny the Minister. But again the Minister ignored that common sense advice.
A short time ago I read a rural magazine wherein the Essex Federation of Agriculture asked an independent lawyer to look at the Bill.
A good lawyer but a good Conservative too.
If he is a good Conservative, that makes his advice more valid.
Hear, hear!

I do not have the article in front of me, but the solicitor from Windsor spoke to the Essex County Federation of Agriculture and put forth the same cautions which we are putting forth today. In fact, coming from St. Thomas, an old railroad city, the solicitor recommended that the farmers of the country should take a little railroad advice. I know what he meant by that. It was a little stop, look and listen. The Minister would do well if he followed the advice we have attempted to give him over the last two years. He would do well if he followed the advice of the legal advisers of the Department of Justice. He would do well if he followed the advice of most agricultural organizations in the country. He would do well if he followed the advice of a solicitor from his own home town.
I recognize that my time is unlimited, but I wanted to use this opportunity to make our position very clear once again. I am certain that our position is very clear across the country; there is no question about that. Hon. Members on this side of the House have put a great deal of energy and effort into trying to inform farm groups in all regions of the country exactly what are the dangers of the Bill. They have done an excellent job. From reading the mail I continue to receive on a daily basis, there is no question in my mind that farmers and people in the agri-food industry know the dangers of the Bill.
1 am extremely disappointed that the Minister has not taken that advice. He has represented the farm community since 1972. That is a long time. It is a very sad day for me, particularly when the message is so clear and he turns his back on the people he represents. If he would have removed the powers to buy and sell, indeed if he would have taken that position from the beginning, we would not be debating the Bill today. I am certain that with the removal of the powers to buy and sell and to engage in joint ventures, we would not be debating the Bill today. I am certain that it would be in place. In doing so, no doubt we would have been farther down the road in providing something which the Canadian agri-food industry needs to increase the exportation of agricultural commodities.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) several questions. In 1979 he was interviewed by a newspaper which has some good farm reporting,
the London Free Press, at which time he was asked what the top priority of his department would be. He replied:
Agriculture exports will be my top priority. It is a springboard from which we can with planning and effort continue to expand our export market opportunities. One tool that will be used to increase exports is the recently announced agriculture export corporation which will sell Canadian foodstuffs abroad.
That is a very good paper. I have several other questions; I will put them as quickly as I can. Members opposite continue to say that the Minister will pit one area of Canada against the other and possibly give special privileges to them by working with Canagrex. Has he considered what Alberta is doing at the present time with subsidies to the canola crushers? Also, there is a $9 a ton freight subsidy. I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that Saskatchewan and Manitoba have made representations to the federal Government asking for the same kind of assistance. They cannot afford that kind of assistance which amounts to almost $49 a ton when you add it all up. That is the assistance they are getting for those products. They are not just for export. This gives them a tremendous advantage over the other canola crushers and producers in other regions. Does he not consider that preferred action? That is Government action.
Does the Hon. Member not know what Tony Saretsky said inthe Agriculture Committee with regard to the Alberta Cattle Commission? I believe it is purebred cattle they deal in, the Canadian Breeders' Association. He said they had to have the operative power to buy and sell and they went back and got the power to buy and sell. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is like Parliament or any other organization. It is a democratic organization. When the majority make a decision to support Canagrex or any other proposition that is put before them, that is democracy in action. Overall they represent about 200,000 people. It is true that some of their members are saying that they have certain reservations about Canagrex and this type of thing.
He challenged me to appear before other boards such as the soybean board, the white bean board, the tobacco board and my own county Federation of Agriculture. I have met them. They still are very strong supporters of Canagrex. I also met with the Canada Pork Council which is still supporting Canagrex and the authority that it has to buy and sell, et cetera.
Also he spoke about my county. I have addressed my own county Federation of Agriculture. He also spoke of a lawyer. Does he realize that when he was a student in law school we were commercial operators picking sweet corn for Green Giant? Therefore we know one another very well.
Does he also realize that the Essex County Federation of Agriculture withdrew their concerns after I addressed them? They said that was satisfactory to them as long as their Member of Parliament and Minister stated it. Is he aware of that? Is he aware that the lawyer he spoke of has been a longtime friend? In a democracy, even friends can disagree.
June 13, 1983

Mr. Speaker, the Minister began by reading, I think very accurately, a response to a comment that I had made to the report in the London Free Press. The accuracy of that report is right on. It is complete. There is no question about the fact that, when I assumed the job as Minister of Agriculture of this country, there was a very definite attempt and thrust to improve agricultural products in the export market.
There were a number of ways to do this. The first way was to give that subject a higher priority in the Department of Agriculture. We began to do that. The other way was to place greater authority and jurisdiction within the Department of Agriculture itself. The Minister knows that if you are dealing in the export market, you are not only dealing with Ag-Canada, you are dealing with Industry, Trade and Commerce, Finance and External Affairs. This becomes pretty cumbersome. You can certainly streamline this and provide greater results for Canadian agriculture if you have more of a consolidation and more of the decision making within Ag-Canada. That is one way. We were working toward that. The Minister cannot deny that; he knows it.
The second way in which we began to move was to increase the number of trade commissioners and trade officers in our embassies around the world. It is very difficult to get these people, no question about it. However, in the very brief time we did hold office we increased the number of trade commissioners and trade officers in our trade offices specifically and totally responsible for the promotion of agriculture products in foreign markets. We did achieve that.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is where the confusion comes in. I did not deal with this in my speech because I was certain someone would ask a question about it. I refer to the area of a special agency or corporation; at that point we really did not know. Certainly a great deal of effort was made within the Department. A couple of submissions were made with respect to the establishment of an agriculture products export agency, call it what you want.
The Minister and indeed some of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party have been attempting to associate me with Canagrex as it is today. That is false. It is not true. I had never heard of "Canagrex". I did not put the name Canagrex on this Bill and the Minister knows it. The Minister can either take the credit or bear the responsibility, depending on what the future holds, for the word Canagrex and the Crown corporation Canagrex. He knows that. There is no doubt about the fact that we were working in that area. We knew that Canadian agriculture had to have an agency or some type of unit which would provide the much needed export credit which had always been denied to agricultural commodities by the Export Development Corporation. Canadian farmers do not have the benefit of the Export Development Corporation. It does not insure for food products and they also needed the benefit of export insurance.
We had no problems with that whatsoever. We were coming to the conclusion that it appeared that in an effort to provide
Canagrex
those export credits and export insurance coverage, we could not do it within a division of Ag-Canada. It was doubtful whether we could do it at an agency level. It appeared that we would probably need a Crown corporation to provide the export credit and the export insurance.
I cannot say any more than that. The Minister knows that for me to say more would be breaking a Privy Council oath. I want him to nod positively to me now that he knows that.
I was not referring to Privy Council.

This is important. The Minister has played political mischief with this question, as have some of my colleagues in the NDP. I am not going to go any further than that, but I will tell you one thing Mr. Speaker. Even if we had brought in Bill C-85 in its present form, even if I would have called it Canagrex, after hearing 32 witnesses before the committee and getting the telegrams, telephone calls and representations which I and other Members of my Party have received, if I sat over there I would have withdrawn months ago the power to buy and sell. I challenge him, dammit, to do the same thing.
Hear, hear!

I did not use the word "Canagrex".

The Western Producer is one of the most widely read magazines in the farmer community.
If I were a farmer, I would not think that there was much difference of opinion between the Hon. Member for Elgin and myself at that stage of the game. That is what I would think if
