1 was a farmer who read the most widely read magazine in the farming community.
The Hon. Member for Elgin also had some reservations. As reported by The Western Producer.
Although Wise says his final decisions on these issues will have to await further briefings, his initial opinions put him in conflict with significant segments of the agriculture community.
That statement was presented to me. The Hon. Member made all kinds of statements and some of them have been put on the record. But when he says that he challenges me after having listened to the witnesses, I challenge him to serve the public, Mr. Speaker, as well as I have and as honestly as I have. How he interprets the witnesses who appeared before the committee in his opinion and how 1 interpret them is my opinion, and we have the right to our own opinions. I interpreted the results of the committee as being that the majority of people who appeared before that committee want the Canadian agricultural export corporation. Research done by my own officials, letters 1 have received, many of which I have not even made public, lead me to make that kind of judgment. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of the agriculture producers in Canada want the Canadian agricultural export corporation. The Hon. Member has a different opinion. That is his right.
Again, 1 must refer to what the Hon. Member for Elgin said in committee: "You have been responsible, you have responded to our requests. It is on the records. I think I can sell this to my caucus." Then he could not sell it to his caucus. What was I to think? He said this after all of the witnesses had appeared before the committee in the final submission to the committee before its results went back to the House of Commons. What was I to think when the official agriculture critic of the Opposition said that at that time? That was before the matter had become politicized.
The brother-in-law of the Hon. Member sitting right across from me, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), who is a potato producer in Manitoba, is a strong supporter of Canagrex in Manitoba. He knows the Canadian agriculture industry.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and I have had conversations about family members who are very dear to me. I do not think that the House of Commons is the place to raise these conversations. I say to the Hon. Minister that he knows very well that my brother-in-law agrees with some parts of Canagrex but has advised him to withdraw others. I would ask the Minister to be honest.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's brother-inlaw and I differ on politics, but we certainly agree on what should be done for agriculture. He has sent me letters and has made public speeches in favour of Canagrex. If he has any reservations that are contrary to my views, I am not aware of them. Any reservations that the Hon. Member's brother-in-law has have not been presented to me. I still respect the Hon. Member's brother-in-law. If he feels that I have offended him,
I withdraw anything that would be offensive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reluctantly put a question to the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) whom I have respected for many years. I find it strange that he did not once mention the news release of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether he questions the sincerity, integrity and credibility of the President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture when the President states in a press release of November 10, 1982:
"Our agricultural industry desperately needs a corporation like Canagrex. It would be criminal to delay putting it in place because of petty politicking,"-
The new release goes on to say:
Barrie stressed that the powers which would be granted to Canagrex are "not extraordinary', and rather than posing a threat to free enterprise, it would be most beneficial to smaller agricultural producer groups, which normally wouldn't be able to crack export markets.
"Canagrex is absolutely essential if we are to fill the gaping void between our potential to produce and manufacture agricultural products for export, and our present performance,"-
This statement was made by the President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, a strong federation, and backs up the strong pleas made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and agricultural federation in Quebec and the National Farmers' Union. These are groups with strong memberships that represent farmers.
I must also ask the Hon. Member if, after having seen the embassy problem, the Petro-Canada problem and the Canagrex problem, this is a turnaround from what was stated in 1979 and what is being stated now, and whether the Opposition does not really know whether it is right to form a Canadian export corporation, as they have been very doubtful on many other things that they might have done.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Kent (Mr. Bossy) asked a number of questions. He did refer to a longtime friend of mine, Ralph Barrie, the President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. I am not so sure who wrote that press release, but I think using the word "criminal" is using a little bit of overkill and is overexaggeration. I am not so sure whether my friend Ralph Barrie would have used that word.
There is no question about the fact that the Ontario Federation of Agriculture led by Mr. Barrie has every right to put forth its views and opinions and its stand on Canagrex. I know what its position is; but on the other hand, looking at the position taken by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, it can be seen that it is supportive of Canagrex but has attached a condition that the Minister cannot comply with. I have challenged the Minister and have invited him to make that commitment to the CFA. He cannot do that. He has had a number of opportunities to do that. He has had a year and a half to do that. Is the Minister asking me to turn my back on nine Provinces and to follow the advice of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture? Is he asking me to turn my back on 28 major national farm organizations plus all of the provincial Governments and turn instead to the Ontario Federation of Agriculture? I cannot do that.
I have talked to my constitutents in Elgin, some whom are supportive of Canagrex. Of course, all of them would feel
June 13, 1983

better if it did not have the power to buy and sell. I have talked to constituents of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I know of one lady, Mrs. Pyke, I believe it is, in that constituency who is very supportive of Canagrex. She would feel better if-
Just one?

Well, there are not many but I know that the Member for Kingston and the Islands does have one constituent who is in favour of it. There is no question about that. Even if I were to stand on my farm in Elgin County, Ontario, with a neighbour who is probably more supportive of Canagrex, as the agriculture critic for this Party and looking at the situation from an Ottawa point of view, I could not turn my back on all this opposition to Canagrex. I could not do that even though I may have a neighbour in southern Ontario who is supportive of it. That would be irresponsible. This is basically the same thing.
From a national point of view one has to listen to the advice not only from Ontario but from eastern and western Canada. I know that advice is mixed, Mr. Speaker. Then you have to decide. I have done that and I have decided in a responsible manner that the proper course of action would be to proceed without the power to buy and sell.
Personally I think the editorial in Farm and Country summed it up-give the power to buy and sell a five-month hoist, come back to Parliament in five years and if you can demonstrate you need it, that is the time to get it. But you must prove that you need the power to buy and sell.
We would not want to hamper in any way, shape or form any measure that would interfere with the process of expanding agricultural products in the export field.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on third reading about the importance of the Bill before the House and the importance of agriculture to our economy.
When I look at the trade performance of Canada around the world, 1 see that in essence the trade missions of this country primarily push manufactured goods and resource products in foreign markets. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the resource associations of our country are very strong lobbyists and have connections with different associations around the world to push their products. I think it is therefore very important that Canadian farmers have an export agency that will push our agricultural products in the world. That exists for some commodities already. In general, the Canadian Wheat Board has been effective in selling our wheat.
I do not understand why the Conservative Party and some other people in the country are apprehensive about giving other farmers the same kind of opportunities that our grain farmers have to sell their products abroad. The legislation before the House today is voluntary; if certain producers do not like the legislation, they need not participate. If they want to sell their tomatoes or cucumbers in a different way, they can
Canagrex
do so. They do not have to participate in Canagrex as it is not a compulsory organization.
After five years the legislation will be reviewed by Parliament and could easily be changed at that time. For those reasons I think we should give the legislation a fair chance.
At the same time, however, I wish the Minister would change a number of things in the Bill. For example, I wish he would allow the farmers of Canada to control and direct Canagrex. This point has been mentioned by the CFA. I wish he would make sure that the farmers of Canada will decide who will sit on the board of directors so that they can run the agency rather than a few bureaucrats in Ottawa doing so. They are often isolated from the reality of the real world. Perhaps that is a radical idea; perhaps it is economic democracy. It is an extension of political democracy into the economic field but I think we must go in that direction. I wish the Minister would agree.
I am afraid he is going to do what so often happens when the federal Government makes appointments to Crown corporations. A lot of old and dear friends are rewarded by being made directors. That is not the direction we want for Canagrex.
I hope the new agency will be successful. Agriculture is so important to everyone in the country.

These are difficult times, not only for Canada but for the whole world, from the economic point of view. We are now experiencing a world-wide recession, and not only that, we also have a lot of unemployment. Here in Canada, agriculture is one of our strongest sectors. Our producers are very good at what they do, very productive, and they need help in seeking international markets for their products. In the House today, we are considering a Bill that will provide that assistance. Mr. Speaker, our producers are faced with a great many problems. The United States and-

-the European Common Market and some other countries in the world are very protectionist about their farmers. The United States has a massive subsidy program of over $12 billion per year to support agricultural production in that country. The Europeans have a tremendous system of price support, price guarantees and subsidies for their farmers. Our grain farmers face tremendous disadvantages because of distance from ports and because other countries pay even more massive subsidies to their grain farmers than we do with the Crow rate.
We need an export agency that will find new markets for our agricultural products. I believe that is very, very important. This legislation will offer the country an opportunity to diversify in agriculture and to take some of the smaller, specialty crops that do not have much clout on the international market and find markets for them. The agency can be the vehicle that will allow the small to participate, allow the small to find a market, allow the small to grow and expand. That is

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
very, very important. This legislation will offer an opportunity to encourage exports.
The other point is that Canagrex is not a very big agency, Mr. Speaker. If I understand correctly, the budget is $4 million per year for the next three years, so it is not going to be a large agency.
Those are some of the reasons I think it is important that Canagrex be given an opportunity. I have also been looking at who is supporting and who is opposing Canagrex. The principle is supported by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and many of the provincial Federations of Agriculture. The Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) mentioned that the Ontario Federation of Agriculture supports it and most provincial marketing boards also support it, as does the National Farmers Union. It is opposed by some of the more reactionary, right-wing and conservative farm organizations, such as the Palliser Wheat Growers Association and organizations of that kind.
In my riding I know that people support orderly marketing and they support the Canadian Wheat Board as being an aggressive sales agency for farmers in world markets. Most farmers want that kind of opportunity for other commodities. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the agency is a voluntary one.
The other point is that the Standing Committee on Agriculture was persuaded to accept an amendment by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) to the effect that the Auditor General may do a comprehensive audit at any time he or she wishes. This will make Canagrex one of the most accountable Crown corporations we have in this country.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that is very important because something which dismays me as an Hon. Member of this House, having been here since 1968, is that I find that federal Crown corporations in the main are not accountable to Members of Parliament. In the main, federal Crown corporations are agencies which look after themselves, which are accountable to a certain Minister or to the federal Government, and I believe that has to change. I feel that to have true parliamentary democracy Crown corporations must be accountable to this institution, to this place.
In my own Province of Saskatchewan, for example, for many, many years now we have had what is called a Crown corporations committee, a committee established by the then Premier, Tommy Douglas, in the CCF Government back in the 1940s or early 1950s. All of the annual reports of the Crown corporations must go to the Crown corporations committee. That committee has the power to call in the presidents of the Crown corporations, and other people from the Crown corporations, and grill them, cross-examine them, and quiz them on what their plans are for the future and how they have handled their work in the years which have gone by.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that is something which this House should be doing as well, making sure that our Crown corporations are much more accountable in the future than they have
been in the past. Perhaps in this piece of legislation we have taken one small step in that direction.
Something which I have already mentioned is that I believe farmers themselves should be on the board of directors. I believe that farmers themselves should choose the people who go on the board of directors of Canagrex. I believe that is very important in terms of understanding the agricultural industry. It is very important in terms of doing what the farmers of this country really want.
I feel, therefore, Mr. Speaker, with a number of reservations, that the legislation before the House is something which should, if properly administered and given a proper chance, be something positive for a lot of the small producers, something positive for a lot of producers who are producing some of the specialty crops in this country. I stress that if they do not like it, they can get out of it. It is voluntary and after five years the House of Commons will once again have an opportunity to review the legislation.
However, I feel it is very important that we give agriculture as much assistance as possible. For too long in this country, government after government has been placing its priorities, its money and its assistance in the baskets of the large company, the large manufacturers, the large resource companies, in the hope this would create a strong and vibrant Canadian economy. That has not happened. One of the sectors which has been very strong throughout all of this has been agriculture and I feel we are going to have to give them more and more assistance. The Economic Development Corporation, for example, does not assist agriculture. It assists the manufacturers. It assists the big in this country. There are many other Crown corporations such as the Canadian Commercial Corporation which will assist manufacturing, processing and resources in this country, but once again will not assist Canadian agriculture.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the House to give this legislation a chance. I appeal to the Minister to be a lot more generous in terms of accepting amendments which Canadian farmers want, to democratize Canagrex, and to keep Canagrex as an agency which is more in touch with the ordinary Canadian producers. I believe that if he does that and is a little more co-operative, then perhaps this is an experiment which can work for each and every one of us.
[ Translation]
This might be a very good thing, not only for our producers across Canada but also for the entire country, in years to come.

Mr. Speaker, is the Hon. Member for York-ton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) aware that the Hon. Member for Elgin, when he was questioned about whether farmers would constitute the majority of the members on the board, expressed strong reservations, and said he thought perhaps it should be people who are in the export business, are knowledgeable in the export business, and so on?
June 13, 1983

Mr. Speaker, I was not aware of that. First of all, I certainly disagree with the Hon. Member for Elgin. I believe farmers should be running this agency. Farmers know best. I believe farmers have a lot of expertise when it comes to the export business. I must say that I am not surprised. We have had a history of Government in this country, whether Liberal or Conservative, where bureaucrats or people from private industry, people with big bucks, have attempted to control Crown corporations and all kinds of Government agencies. When the Hon. Member makes that kind of statement it is not a surprise at all to me, Mr. Speaker.
However, I feel we must now go in the other direction.We must move towards really democratizing this country, making sure that ordinary workers, farmers and consumers, ordinary people, will be able to make important economic decisions in Canada. I believe for all too long we have tended to think that the important ecnomic decisions should be made by people who have the big bucks. If you are wealthy, if you are the president of a company, all of a sudden you have tremendous credibility. Company presidents and others in this country who have alot of money, Mr. Speaker, the extreme rich and the privileged of this country, have over the years made many, many mistakes. I would trust the farmers and the ordinary workers a lot more than I would trust the corporate elite in this country. Perhaps in the next few years we will recognize that people with certain experience in the big business community are not the best thing for the ordinary citizens of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I really rise on a point of order rather than to pose a question to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), because I believe he was somewhat misled. I was having a discussion with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister in an effort to reach some type of agreement in the reduction in time required for speakers and enable us to get more people on. I thought I heard the Minister quote an article where I said I did not want farmers on the board. That, of course, is very inaccurate. It is untrue. I said that the best thing that we could do is to make certain that on the board are those people who were the most qualified to serve on that board in the export field. So much the better if we can get those kinds of people from the farm industry. That is to say, I believe the best route to go is that the people who serve on that board should be the people most qualified to do so. There was certainly nothing in my thoughts that farmers should not be on that board. The Minister knows that.

Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I will send the Hon. Member the document where he was quoted. I am quoting from a document which says he does not agree with the former Government's proposal that the export agency be controlled by farmer members of the board. "He said his priority will be to have salesmen and marketing specialists on the board and any qualification as a producer
will be secondary. This will run counter to the strong view of the Canadian Federatioan of Agriculture which resisted the initial proposal for an export agency until it has a commitment from Mr. Whelan that a majority of members would be farmers." I am quoting.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what document the Minister is quoting from, but I think perhaps it would be a good idea if he would send it across to me and I could determine its accuracy.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, by calling for the final day of supply as House business tomorrow, June 14, the Government has foreclosed Supplementary Estimates A. The Committees of this House have had precious little time to deal with these Estimates. There were no financial figures available for Canadair Limited until June 7. On that date the Committee managed to have only two meetings. Members have had virtually no opportunity to inquire into the need for that corporation to receive another $240 million.
The effect of tomorrow being an Opposition day totally prevents a realistic parliamentary inquiry into this Supplementary Estimate. The Committee has had no opportunity to look at de Havilland. The proper thing for the Government to do, if it believes in full disclosure and Parliament looking after the spending of money, is to delay the Opposition day until the week of June 27. That would be in accordance with precedent.
In the alternative, if the Government should specifically insist on an Opposition day tomorrow, it should withdraw the Estimates for Canadair and de Havilland, file new Supplementary Estimates, and allow the parliamentary process to work so that Parliament can have a chance to find out whether we should spend this money or not.

Madam Speaker, I want to remind this House that while the excitement of the Tory Convention dominated the news media last week, perhaps rightly so, the unemployment statistics came out as well. We must not forget amongst all this excitement that a great deal of human suffering continues in Canada. Unemployment is up since last year, and two things have been clearly indicated by these statistics. We have a very serious continuing problem of long-term unemployment, while the Government has brought in employment programs of short-term nature. Secondly, student unemployment this summer is up to an historic high. One in every five students seeking a job this summer cannot find work.
Now that the Liberal Government, in its last budget, shifted to the right in an attempt to undercut the Tory businessman style of politics, 1 call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to try to undercut the Tories' claim of compassion, by doing something real and immediate for students this summer.

subsubtopic: BALTIC AND UKRAINIAN ECUMENICAL REMEMBRANCE SERVICE
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, last week a large group of people held an ecumenical service at Notre Dame Basilica in Ottawa to commemorate the
hiderous suffering of the Baltic-Ukrainian nations and the fiftieth anniversary of the famine in the Ukraine.
Archbishop Maxim Hermaniuk reminded us that approximately seven million human beings were murdered in the 1932-33 famine because they had dared to resist Joseph Stalin's collectivization of their farms. Their grain and vegetables were seized and, incredibly, exported to gain hard currency for the Soviet Union. In short, it was a merciless and deliberate act of genocide. The Right Rev. Bishop Vasylij of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church recounted that 1,150 priests, 30 bishops, and thousands of lay members of his church were murdered during the 1930s in Stalin's attack on religion.
It was also pointed out to those of us present that between 1941 and 1953 more than one million Balts were deported from their homelands by Soviet Communists.
The service was sponsored by the Ottawa branches of the Estonian Society, the Latvian National Federation, the Lithuanian Canadian Community and the Ukrainian Canadian Committee, supported by the Byelorussian Canadian Alliance, the Czechoslovak National Association, the Hungarian Bartock Society, the Polish Congress, and the Slovak National League.

subsubtopic: EXECUTION OF FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF HUNGARY- TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on June 16, 1958, the former Prime Minister of Hungary and his cabinet colleagues were executed for their role in the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. Their remains, along with those of the many others similarly put to death, were buried by the authorities in numbered graves. The location of these burial sites remains a state secret to this day.
On the eve of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the execution of Mr. Nagy and his associates, the Canadian Government should appeal to the Hungarian Regime to observe basic human decency and adhere to the principles of human rights embodied in the Helsinki Agreement's Final Act, by responding to repeated pleas for the identification of the graves and for permission to reinter the remains at a final resting place of their survivors' own choosing.
At the same time, of course, the Canadian Government should always be doing everything it can to protest and help abate the oppression and persecution of current dissidents within the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, and the Baltic States. In particular may I remind the Government of the plight of two young women, Olha Heyko and Iryna Ratushyn-ska, who face 12 years' imprisonment each for "anti-Soviet agitation and propaganda", and remind the Government of the need for representations to be made on their behalf.

subsubtopic: RESTRUCTURING OF EAST COAST FISHING INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I had hoped to direct my question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans with whom I had discussions about the Atlantic fisheries. In his absence, perhaps the Chairman of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Development, or even the Prime Minister, could indicate the latest view of the Government on the restructuring of the fleet and the refinancing of the Atlantic fishing industry.
The Prime Minister, if he chooses to answer, I am sure knows that delay in this case is the deadliest form of denial. No one connected with this industry can have any certainty of purpose, and there are widespread fears that the Government is withholding its assistance to the industry in order to force the companies into a position where they may have to be nationalized.
I am sure that the Government is aware that the problems created by such an atmosphere of uncertainty in the industry must be addressed, particularly when the press has speculated that the aid will not be given until some time in July.
Can the Prime Minister, or someone in his Cabinet, tell the House and the country whether or not the Government will address the problem quickly? Is it in fact negotiating with the provincial Governments in order to transfer the problem there in return for several hundreds of millions of dollars, so that the provincial Governments will have to deal with problems which, according to speculation, could involve the closing of some individual plants?

Madam Speaker, I would only say Amen, to the first part of the question. It is a matter which I have been following quite closely in Cabinet for some time. I think the Hon. Member is expressing the kind of distress that I have also found on this side, that the matter has taken such a long period of time to settle.
The Government's intentions were made known well before the turn of the year. The rest has been a matter of very lengthy negotiations, not amongst ourselves since the Cabinet took the position many months ago, but because we did have to see the provincial Governments. We had to see the people in the industry, and we had to meet the representatives of the fishermen themselves.
I have in mind a recent agreement that was reached between our Minister and the Newfoundland Minister of Fisheries, only to be rejected by the provincial Cabinet. Therefore we had to go back to square one and look for other ways of making improvements to the whole fishing industry in a way which, hopefully, would be conductive to co-operation between
the federal and provincial Governments, the business side and the fishermen's side, meaning the unions.
I repeat that it is not for want of desire or even intent on the part of the Government; it is because the negotiating process itself is a very lengthy one, as the Hon. Member must know from experience, when trying to get provincial Governments to agree amongst themselves and then with us.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed either to the Prime Minister of the Chairman of the Economic Development Committee, who has arrived in the Chamber. I appreciate the Prime Minister's answer. I want to bring up another specific matter of concern in the Atlantic region, namely, the fate of the small independent processors and co-ops who have provided a degree of competition and stability to the industry in the past. I am thinking of some companies of which the Minister knows, such as Connors Brothers, United Maritime Fish, Abriel Fisheries Ltd., and so on. Anyone who thinks that the entire Atlantic fishery is in crisis should realize that, out of a total of 250 fish plants in Nova Scotia, 230 have done well.
What will happen in the future to some of these small independent processors who have been absorbed by the big conglomerates and dragged into financial ruin? Can the Minister give us some indication that the position of these independents will be protected? How does he propose to do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member indicated, some of the small independents have done very well indeed. I am confident that they will continue to do so within a restructured fishery. As the Prime Minister has indicated, negotiations are proceeding at this very moment, as effectively as they have been for some months.
Furthermore, as the Hon. Member knows, the matter is extremely complex. There has to be a solution which will protect all of these interests and which will make the fishery economical and viable in the long term.

Madam Speaker,
I simply want to ask the Minister to assure us that, besides the inevitable delays and negotiations that the Prime Minister has referred to, the Cabinet committee members concerned have resolved any differences of opinion that they have, and are no longer split as reports have indicated, and that there will in fact be something done before July?

Madam Speaker, may I direct my question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who,
I believe, will share my disappointment and concern with respect to the statistics revealed by the Canadian Government's survey of the labour force for the last six months. speechtext: Madam Speaker, always the question is what is in the eye of the beholder. One-third of our GNP is generated by foreign trade, and one out of every four jobs in dependent upon foreign trade. Given the fact that 70 per cent of Canada's export market is in the United States, is the Government planning any new sets of arrangements with the United States which, while ensuring our own Canadian sovereignty, will also ensure secured access to vital American markets?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Government is seeing its Ministers cross the border almost in a perpetual fashion.

Six months later, and given Canada's continuing need for expanded markets to broaden its international trading base and thereby increase job creation in Canada, can the Prime Minister tell the House at this time, specifically six months later, what new trade arrangements have been made or are being negotiated as a result of the Prime Minister's and his other Ministers' visits to the Asian Pacific Rim?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

Where is he?

Member he shares that view with many people on this side, and that is why the Minister for international trade has had an extended trip to the Pacific Rim countries. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I disagree with the Hon. Member's suggestion that we have failed to consider the main recommendations of the McDonald Commission. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in so far as the point in the former question about the power of the Minister in relation to the power of the Director is concerned, the system composed in the legislation, copied incidentally from Australian parliamentary democracy which works very well, was designed to assure that in moving the agency from the RCMP where there was considerable public assurance and confidence that there was no partisan abuse of the agency it provided for the direction and safeguard that the Director would have the final authority only in relation to a particular case, not in relation to the over-all direction of the agency. subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF CAST SHIPPING GROUP-GOVERNMENT APPROVAL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. It appeared that it would have been useful, prior to Cabinet taking a decision with respect to a Canadian National takeover of Cast, that the combines investigation hearings into that matter should have been completed, that the CTC hearings should have been completed, and that, at the very minimum, the Standing Committee on Transport should have had an opportunity to examine further the matters surrounding this situation. Could the Minister indicate whether or not Cabinet has now issued an Order in Council authorizing Canadian National's full takeover the Cast and its group?

subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF CAST SHIPPING GROUP-GOVERNMENT APPROVAL
speechtext:
Yes, Madam Speaker, indeed Cabinet authorized CN to negotiate an alliance of some kind with Cast, but the deal has not yet been done. The order in council is an authorization to negotiate on certain terms.
On the subject raised by my Hon. friend, first on the combines investigation, I already answered that question saying that I had consulted with the Minister responsible who told me there was no objection to any negotiation. On the second point, the CTC inquiry, it is the practice for both the private and public sector in Canada to conclude first and then refer to the CTC for approval or denial. That is the normal practice. We proceeded in that way in the knowledge that, in a previous case, the acquisition of Dart by CP ships, on the one-third basis, the CTC rendered a favourable decision, justified by the requirements of vertical integration. With respect to the committee, my hon. friend is a member of it. He can question the President of CNR at any time.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES REQUEST TO TEST CRUISE MISSILE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Prime Minister. We have been informed today that the United States has in fact asked for approval to test the Cruise missile in Canada. The communique issued by the Minister of National Defence indicates two things. The first is that the proposed test program falls within the terms of the Canada-U.S. test and evaluation
program agreement. And, in a somewhat contradictory way, the Minister indicates that officials of the Department of National Defence will now begin an assessment of the proposed test program. Given that there appears to be some contradiction, 1 would like to ask the Prime Minister if the proposal submitted by the U.S. falls within the terms foursquare of the agreement signed between Canada and the United States. Will the review process that is to be undertaken be undertaken in such a way as to allow for public input?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES REQUEST TO TEST CRUISE MISSILE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is correct. There was a request made this morning to the Minister of National Defence. He consulted with me and we did announce this morning that the request had been received.
As to the question the Hon. Member puts, I must point out to him that the weapons testing agreement that had been signed many months ago with the United States was an umbrella agreement. What the Minister is stating now is that the request we have fits within that umbrella agreement. In other words, it is not a request for the test that would be made outside of the agreement or outside of the over-all understanding.
The purpose for the Minister and his Department now will be to examine and to assess, as the Minister says, the precise request, now that he has ascertained that it comes under the agreement. That is all that the Hon. Member's first paragraph or first quotation means, that it is within the terms of the umbrella agreement. But there was never any general understanding or particular one that everything submitted to us within the umbrella agreement would be agreed to. Now we have to look at each specific test, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister further if it will be possible for the submission that has now been received by the Canadian Government to be made available to the Members of the House of Commons, as was the test agreement, in order that we can determine, on behalf of the people whom we represent, what effect this particular proposal or set of proposals will have on the communities or areas that will be affected by the testing. Further, I ask him again if there will be further opportunity for public input prior to the Government making a final decision.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot say whether the request itself could be made public. I have seen it; I have not read it. I would think that is a question on which I would have to seek advice.
As to the concern of the Hon. Member, I do not think he has to wait to see any fine print to make up his mind as to whether we should test the Cruise or not. The parameters are well known. It is a non-armed missile. It is a request which comes
June 13, 1983

under the two-track decision, or at least it is a request which Cabinet is considering as related to the two-track decision of NATO taken in December, 1979, and obviously it will involve testing over some part of Canada. If the Hon. Member needs more details to know whether he is in favour of it or opposed to it, perhaps he could ask me what those details are and I would attempt to give him the answer.

Madam Speaker, 1 personally do not require any further information to determine that I am opposed to it. My concern is that the public of Canada should be made fully aware of the implications of the announcement which was made today.

Madam Speaker, is there any doubt in the mind of the Prime Minister that Canada has now committed itself fully to promote Cruise testing within this umbrella agreement as submitted by the U.S. Government to the Canadian Government, as of today's announcement?
