Canagrex

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Whelan that Bill C-85, an Act to establish a corporation called Canagrex to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agricultural and food products in Canada, be read a third time and do pass.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be taking part in the debate on third reading of this Bill, and I am looking forward to the moment when the question will be put. We are going to have a chance to do something positive for Canada. This will be another step towards a stronger Canada and a more prosperous future.
This morning, I was very pleased to hear the Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) express his agreement with the principle of Canagrex. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that, with a few exceptions, we have varying views on the way this Bill should be implemented. However, I wonder who understands agriculture and the farmer. Is it the consumer? Is it the editorial writers or the organizations that stand up for the rights of farmers in this country?
Mr. Speaker, I think that those in the best position to judge are the large organizations that defend the interests of our producers. When I sat on the Standing Committee on Agriculture, almost all of these organizations supported this legislation aimed at exporting Canadian agricultural products throughout the world. I noticed that all provincial organizations and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and almost all its branches were almost totally in support of the Bill's concept.
Nowdays, it is fashionable to be aggressive and to criticize pratically everything. However, if we are to progress, we must make constructive decisions and have confidence in the future. This legislation is based on the confidence we have in our farmers, processors and business people, and on our confidence in our natural ability to produce and market even more than we are doing at the present time.
This legislation offers Canadians in the agri-food industry a set of new mechanisms that will help them compete on foreign markets. These objectives deserve our support, Mr. Speaker. On many occasions, the Minister has said that he would like to see an agricultural export corporation very shortly. He has said this so many times and for so long, that some people wondered whether the Bill would ever be passed at all. Quite sincerely, I am very glad to see that we are now seeing the light at the end of the tunnel, and that Canagrex has almost become a reality.

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on Agriculture sat for four months. We have been sitting for hours to consider the third reading and final stages of this legislation. Thirty-two or 37 different groups took part in our discussions. All the major organizations contributed their ideas, and today, I must say that, as I said earlier, all the provincial federations, all those who are in fact working in the agri-food industry, are practically unanimous in saying that the corporation is necessary. Once again, I would like to say that we have some differences as to the implementation of this legislation, but it would seem that on the whole, most people approve of this legislation, which will have a very positive effect on the agricultural industry.
With a $12.3 million budget for three years, a Board of 11 Directors and a staff of 20, Canagrex will be a small but powerful corporation whose main role will be to act as catalyst between foreign buyers and Canada's producers, processors and exporters. It will be particularly useful to small businesses by helping them steer through the uncharted waters of new foreign markets. As one of our colleagues from Prince Edward Island so aptly put it last week, we in this country have major organizations which look after our main crops, but we also have very remote regions which need that assistance to be more dynamic, more productive, and to export more. During his trips abroad, the Minister soon became convinced that there was a need for such services, and he constantly noticed that a demand for our food products did exist. Unfortunately, nothing was being done to translate that demand into export orders. No one bothered to find out whether the necessary measures were being taken to identify those markets and follow through to the final sale.
The Minister is not saying that our export efforts have failed, for Canada's agricultural food export industry is strong and flourishing, as evidenced by the fact that last year we exported close to $9 billion worth of agricultural products and had a trade balance surplus of $3.1 billion. In spite of that, a number of sectors of the agricultural food industry throughout Canada could be improved if appropriate steps were taken to find new markets for our increasing production.
Canada needs exports because they are at the core of our economic activities. They are vital for our economy as a whole. Since our domestic market is rather small and cannot absorb everything we can produce, we must have foreign markets to achieve our full productive capacity as a nation and as individuals. In addition, Canada being one of the three or four countries which export more food than they import, it has the obligation, generally speaking, of helping others who increasingly suffer from famine. On a per capita basis, we have five times more agricultural land than the world average. It would be a shame to leave that land fallow when hundreds of millions of people are going hungry and would like our food.
I should think there is no need for me to dwell on these points because they are rather obvious. I would simply like to mention a few features of the new corporation and emphasize the guarantees that Canagrex will continue to serve the agricultural food industry.
As Hon. Members know, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Canagrex is to promote, facilitate and, to a limited extent, engage in exports of agricultural and food products. Most members of the Board of Directors of Canagrex will come from the private sector and the President will be responsible for the operations. He or she will be on the Board of Directors and will exercise the duties assigned to the Board.
Canagrex will help private businesses as well as marketing councils and co-operatives in various ways such as financial services through loans or guarantees, advertising, consultation and information facilities, the search for markets, joint undertakings, as well as through grants or contributions to help develop and promote products, and provide the necessary infrastructure. Practically every group which appeared before the Standing Committee agreed on the need for Canagrex to provide credit, advertising and market identification services. Other groups, however, questioned the need for Canagrex to engage in the export trade. They feared that such an initiative could result in unfair competition with the private sector. I believe that those concerns are adequately met by the amendments to the Bill, as I intend to demonstrate.
In addition to the fact that most members of the board will be appointed from the private sector, a Policy Advisory Committee will be established. It will include representatives from all parts of the Canadian agri-food industry. Thus, Canagrex will benefit from the experience and the advice of the private and public sectors. Canagrex will not import, export or process products on its own initiative. It is not a marketing cooperative. Its services will only be provided on a voluntary basis. The most important amendment made to the Bill is probably the restriction placed on the powers of Canagrex to engage in the export trade. The Bill clearly states that Canagrex will not engage in the export of Canadian agricultural and food products to other countries except from state to state or in cooperation with, at the request of or jointly with the private sector.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the Canagrex concept is similar to what many other countries have already done to increase their share of the agri-food export market. As the Minister of Agriculture has pointed out this morning, we already have in Canada large organizations for the grain industry, such as the Canadian Wheat Board in Western Canada. This sector of the agricultural industry is very well organized and the Canadian Wheat Board has the same powers to purchase and export as Canagrex will have. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I find it surprising that so many Members opposite are shocked that the Minister is making a praiseworthy effort to give Canagrex the same privileges and the
June 13, 1983

same rights so that it may increase our export trade throughout the world. This is not a plot aimed at taking over the industry, as several Members opposite have said, but rather a response to meet acknowledged needs. I am firmly convinced that Canagrex will meet a real need and that it will give Canada the means to fill the ever increasing gap between the Canadian agri-food sector and our competitors. Reference was also made this morning to other countries which use similar instruments and are becoming increasingly aggressive on the export market.
I noticed recently that England, France, the United States and Mexico now have legislation to provide similar tools to Canagrex and are becoming increasingly aggressive on the export markets. In Canada, we are told to be very careful and to ask other people to deal with the problem. I am not blaming the system, Mr. Speaker. In the past, many people have tried to export our agricultural products, and as I said earlier, who knows agriculture better? Is it the merchants, the farmers or the agricultural organizations? I seriously wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the major agricultural organizations are really more knowledgeable about the needs of the Canadian farmer and the needs of the export and foreign markets.
So, personally, I am not distressed about the fact that powers are to be given to that corporation, and that such powers will also be restricted. The day Canagrex will be going abroad to identify trading opportunities, it will inform all the producers and processers who are in a position to develop such opportunities by themselves, in co-operation with Canagrex.
It is clearly provided in the Bill that Canagrex will not handle products that come under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Dairy Commission, so long as it has not been requested to do so. Whenever this will prove useful, Canagrex will resort to existing government services, such as those of trade commissioners.
I would like again to deal with the matter of checks on Canagrex activities, and suggest that this House has no cause for concern over the powers which will allow Canagrex to discharge the following responsibilities. First, Canagrex will have to identify and supply information on markets, and supply promotional information services.
Mr. Speaker, I see no production problem in this country at present, but we do have selling and exporting difficulties. I appreciate the fact that Canagrex will provide promotional and informational services that will be very important to farmers, namely with respect to the granting of loans and guarantees and the underwriting of insurance. When I was working with the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I have been aware all along that several of my colleagues were suggesting that Canagrex, or whatever corporation is to be established, should grant loans, assign guarantees and underwrite insurance. In my view, those requirements are essential to that corporation's efficiency, because on export markets
Canagrex
now the majority of our producers do not have the know-how and expertise needed to penetrate those markets, and often those who have tried in the past, for a lack of know-how or information, have simply gone bankrupt or otherwise obtained contracts that were not profitable, where buyers failed to pay their debt or failed to pay for the products that were purchased.
Canagrex should also enter into joint ventures with private companies. It will act as a Crown agent in the negotiation of contracts between governments. The trend today in international trade, is for nations to deal on the government level. We have seen how North-African nations, other Arab countries and even Mexico, and the USSR are increasingly anxious to deal directly with government-controlled corporations. So, in my view, it is in Canada's best interests to have this corporation, which will be limited, which will have an annual budget and which will be subject every year to the Auditor General's examination.
Therefore, I want to suggest to my colleague opposite that both the grain industry and the Canadian Dairy Commission will remain outside the jurisdiction of the Canagrex corporation. Whenever Canagrex will be collecting products for an export contract, it will use public adjudicators and act in such a way as not to affect the competitive position of any agri-food export operation. It will not duplicate the work of the Canadian Wheat Board, as I said, nor that of the Canadian Dairy Commission. It will handle products falling under these organizations only at their request.
Five years after its inception, the performance of Canagrex will be subject to a complete review by the Standing Committee on Agriculture. As a further guarantee, as I said, the Auditor General can proceed to an exhaustive audit of the corporation's operations.
Indeed, in his latest report, the Auditor General has already pointed to the merits of Canagrex which, even before being established, was already taking very practical steps to become very dynamic and eliminate any concern it may have aroused.
To my mind, those clauses provide an overall protection for the private sector and the taxpayers. Indeed, we have taken the necessary steps to make sure that Canagrex will exercise its powers in a responsible manner.
Canagrex will provide tremendous opportunities especially with regard to products other than our traditional exports- wheat, feed crops, oilseeds and meat. A few commodities identified in joint studies carried out by Agriculture Canada and Industry, Trade and Commerce also include maple syrup, field peas, honey and other horticultural products.
I should like to add, Mr. Speaker, as one of my colleagues has said it so well last week, we have many productions in this country, especially at the horticultural level where producers, as opposed to other areas, have a surplus and they will now be in a position to be more dynamic on world markets. And also

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
consider Mr. Speaker, that Canagrex should be most helpful with respect to all commodities especially in the central and eastern areas of the country so that we may become more dynamic on export markets and help reduce our trade balance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would some Hon. Members care to address questions to the speaker who has just resumed his seat.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order rather than to question the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Dionne). I do so in an effort to expedite the debate this afternoon. I have had some discussion with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). We would like to propose that our two or three remaining 20-minute periods this afternoon before 5.45 p.m. be split so that we can put forward two speakers. I recognize that the Minister or any Member of the House will reserve his or her right to utilize ten minutes in the form of questions. As far as House rules are concerned, Mr. Speaker, I realize that you have some difficulty with that. The responsibility would be placed on Members of my Party to discipline themselves and to watch the clock.
We would have to proceed on the basis of unanimous consent. Discussions have been held, and 1 think the Minister would agree with that proposal. If the House agrees, we would appreciate it very much.
Mr. Speaker, we have no objections on this side as long as they divide the 20 minutes amongst themselves and agree not to use any more than 20 minutes between the two speakers.
Mr. Speaker, we are quite prepared to support this recommendation in order to provide an opportunity for the maximum of speakers on this critical topic.

Mr. Speaker, first 1 want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) the agriculture critic for our Party, for doing such an outstanding job in the presentation of the facts with respect to his position, our Party's position and the farmers' position as it relates to Canagrex. I believe it was a forthright and courageous statement which was presented with a great deal of integrity. I support his position totally.
The last speaker stated that Canagrex has but $12.6 million as a budget. Having been in the House for some 10 ten years now, I am very well aware of the fact that there are two ways by which that budget could be supplemented indefinitely at any time when it suits the Minister of the day. With approval from Treasury Board, he can get any additional amount of money which may be required and we shall later consider it in Supplementary Estimates. Therefore, the $12.6 million is not a constraining factor at this point in time.
Second, the Hon. Member referred to instruments of legislation which are applied in the United States in situations which require public treatment for the disposition of agricultural products. Yes, they have them but not in the socialistic form in which they now exist in Canagrex. Any suggestion that
they are in such a form there is entirely deceptive as far as the public and Canadian farmers are concerned.
I think it is interesting to note that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has agreed that he will support this Bill. At the same time he has expressed certain reservations about the fashion in which it will be done. He pleads for caution and good judgment in the administration of the Bill after it is passed. In fact, he reflects the position which many farm organizations in the West, particularly in Saskatchewan, have taken in their reserved judgment as to what the real value of this Bill is. I think the Minister of Agriculture would be very well advised at this time to give further consideration to the reservations expressed by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville and a multitude of other farm organizations. If the Minister would reflect on the minutes of the meeting, he would see that the New Brunswick Potato Agency expressed strong opposition to the opportunity which this Bill would extend to the Government. It did not want the joint venture aspect of this Bill. It does in fact support the principles which this Bill suggests but it does not support the vehicles which we are legislating to make the Bill active. For instance, I have been pressing since my earliest Agriculture Committee meeting in this House for an international capability for the extension of our trade in agricultural products abroad. I strongly disagree with the vehicle which the Minister is going to use. In discussing this particular facet of the Bill I will explain my objections. I pleaded for more agricultural representation in the consulates of the world to represent Canadian trade. In 1972, in the earliest Agriculture Committee which I attended, I was advised that Canada has one fulltime agricultural representative in our consulates abroad. We had just one.
I will acknowledge that there has been a further extension of that service and that we do now have some five official representatives in our embassies abroad. As well, we have some seconded people and some part-time people representing agricultural trade abroad. But we are still not universally represented for trade in this agricultural world which demands food.
I do in fact support the principle that we put greater emphasis on the international trade aspect and the extension of that capability world-wide. I do not support the concept that we put two bureaucracies in place which will find themselves in conflict, one from Agriculture and one from Industry, Trade and Commerce, or whatever Department now looks after that in this confused state of portfolio responsibilities.
I do support the principle of export credits and the principle of export insurance, but I do not support the concept that this should be extended to a Crown corporation. I think rather that it should be extended to traders in food in Canada who are recognized in the rest of the world. I do not suggest that it should go through a Crown corporation.
I do suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we need these three things. I repeat, we need export credit, export insurance and
June 13, 1983

agricultural expertise in our consulate representation abroad. We do need a capability to facilitate, to expedite and to finalize certain trade opportunities, but not a Crown corporation of the magnitude that is being put in place. I do suggest that we need influence for orderly markets, but I do not suggest that we legislate upon farmers of this land the criteria by which they may be able to produce and trade, which is what this Bill will do.
The Minister has tried to hide behind the fact that he really will not be doing much buying and selling, that he will not be getting any land, that he will not be producing anything, yet he insists on a joint venture. This is an indirect vehicle for the acquisition of land and the production of crops. That is the mildest way in which we can describe it. This Corporation will also allow the extension of this capability into the processing, marketing, buying and selling. The whole field of agriculture is engulfed. The Minister has been extending unto himself the capability of participation in agriculture from the sod to the starving millions of this world in every aspect of agricultural production, management, processing and sales. I do not like that aspect of this Bill.
1 want to draw to the Speaker's attention and to the attention of this House that virtually every agricultural ministry in every provincial Government in Canada has expressed reservations. While supporting the three principles which I first enunciated, these ministries have asked that he amend and qualify the method of application and eliminate some of the vehicles the Minister proposes to put in place, particularly as it relates to joint ventures and to the Crown corporation.
The Minister has become personal when he referred to the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). I, too, have had conversation with the gentleman to whom the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) referred, and he did, as I do, agree with the principles contained in this Bill. But the Hon. Member objected to the method of application of the principles to the field of agriculture and their invasion of the privacy of the farmer, the marketing board and the market in general. This we cannot tolerate, and the misrepresentation and reflection upon a Member of this House is something which we hope to see no more.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.
The Hon. Member is imputing motives in saying that 1 said something that would degrade anyone at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
Just a minute, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The Minister is entering into an argument with regard to what was said or not said. I believe we have an agreement with regard to time. There will be a period for an exchange of questions at the end, and 1 suggest the Minister reserve his comments until then. The Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain).

Mr. Speaker, in closing I simply want to say, as I leave the next ten minutes to the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), yes, help finance, help
Canagrex
insure, help market but do not enter farming through joint ventures. Do not put in place a Crown corporation. Do not get into buy and sell activities. It is the vehicle to which the farmers have objected, not the principle.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) for the House order so that more Members can participate in this debate under this closure motion until the bells start to ring at 5.45 p.m. Admittedly, a 20-minute loaf is better than a ten-minute loaf, but usually I like the full loaf. Usually I do not have notes and take my full time. This is a ten-minute rule which I do not want to abuse. I want to say though that it is a very innovative procedure that should be adopted more often. It allows more Members to speak when this type of restrained debate is in place. I thank the Minister very much for this order and those Members who co-operated.
I want to say very briefly, and without trying to cause any problem in the House in the ten minutes I have allotted to me, that the Government, in my humble opinion, has been erroneous in its defence of Canagrex on three major points. First, the Government has suggested that the agriculture industry needs a Crown corporation as extensive as Canagrex and that it ought to play that great a role in the industry.
Second, the Government has assured the House and the public that under the provisions of Bill C-85 Canagrex will be sufficiently accountable to Parliament and that it will not become another expensive drain on the public purse.
Third, the Government has claimed that the majority of the agriculture industry in Canada is in favour of Canagrex as it is now proposed. I am not talking about principles but all the details that are in the Bill, many of which my friend from Carleton-Charlotte has touched upon.
I suggest to you that these three areas, these assertions of the Government, are highly suspect. They are in reality traverses of the truth, figments of fabrication and really do dishonour to honesty. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the agriculture industry is not in need of a brand new corporation with such extensive potential for intervention.
Virtually all Parties in the House recognize the fine track record of private export and marketing endeavours to date. They also recognize the potential for even further improvement of marketing and export management. Thus there is room for a government body, no doubt about that, to come in and play an important role, and we, the Opposition, have endorsed those portions of the Bill that "promote and facilitate" powers in the Canagrex Bill. We have supported ideas of credits and insurance, but we refuse to endorse the provisions of the Bill which would allow Canagrex to engage in the buying and selling of agricultural products.
Much has been said on the topic of these powers. The issue came up in committee, and indeed the Government has accepted amendments that would restrict these powers in part,

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
but are they restrictive enough? The restrictions do not alleviate the concern that Canagrex may end up participating in the agricultural market not only as a facilitator for private deals, as the Government suggests will be the case, but also as a direct participant itself. We, the Opposition, are not satisfied that such concern is sufficiently alleviated. The powers are there and they can be used. If they can be used, in our humble opinion they can be abused.
Subsection 4(1 )(d) as reported from committee allowed Canagrex to "enter into contracts with foreign governments to provide agricultural products", and to "enter into subcontracts with Canadian enterprises or individuals ... for the provision to foreign governments of any of the products and services that Canagrex has itself contracted to provide".
Deciphered somewhat, this subsection allows Canagrex to engage in extensive buying and selling of agricultural products. Perhaps this is a far-out example but let me put it in far-out terms so that we understand what we are doing. If Canagrex contracted to sell five mangoes to the Government of Upper Volta-my voice is somewhat hoarse today; I need a mango to clear it in view of the activities of the last few days-it would then have the power to make good that contract by buying those mangoes from Canadian producers. This may sound relatively harmless. But what if the Government were to contract to sell Upper Volta not five but five million mangoes and chose to purchase them exclusively from the mango producers of one Province or region? I am using mangoes as my example so that I will not have to worry about casting aspersions on any part of the productivity of the country, because I do not think we produce a heck of a lot. The potential implications of Government participation in buying and selling become more clear. Alternatively, what if Canagrex were to decide to seek bids from Canadian producers to supply the mangoes? The result would be increased domestic competition among Canadian producers that would drive prices down. Canagrex could also wind up taking profits which would otherwise end up in the hands of producers.
Perhaps the Government will tell us that Canagrex is not designed to do any of this, that it is not within the spirit of Bill C-85. This is what the Government has more or less said. We all know, if the power is there under the letter of the law in the Bill, that potentially it can be done.
In looking at legislation, legislators have to look at any new Bill to see what its potential may be, not just at the best wishes of the Minister no matter how sincere, assuming the best wishes and sincerity of this Minister. We have to look at the letter of the law in the Bill to see what is its potential, and we say that the potential is there.
In the case of Canagrex, the Government tells us that the corporation will use its buy and sell powers only in very narrowly defined ways. However, the Bill as it now stands would enable a Crown corporation to play a significant trading role in the agricultural markets of Canada. We know too well how governments like to expand and increase their powers. For example, let us look at Petro-Canada which was supposed to
be a window on the industry, a minor observer in the petroleum world. Now it has become a major participant in the petroleum industry itself. We have seen other examples of extensive government intervention in all sorts of industries, and that is our fear here.
We are very much against the buy and sell provisions. The proposed power to enter into joint ventures is not as harmless as the Government would lead us to believe. Again the problems of patronage and favouritism could arise. The potential is there. Any businessman knows that a government agency is a powerful competitor. The absence of strict profit-loss motives and the access to public funds give government corporations a decided advantage over other firms in an industry. Therefore, by picking and choosing its partners in joint ventures, Canagrex could promote the welfare of certain produces while hurting others.
In short, the restrictions placed upon the powers of Canagrex to buy and sell agricultural products are not sufficient. The simple fact is that the Government could still become a trading partner in the agricultural export business and an active producer and processor in the domestic industry. We cannot allow the Government to extend another long and harmful tentacle into the private sector which, ironically, is a sector that is basically productive. There are problems but it is alive and well without Canagrex. With Canagrex our fear is that even with the best of intentions it could become the chloroform of the industry rather than the catalyst for growth which is so necessary.
There is a temptation for Ministers here in Ottawa at the head of large Departments to think that they know best. We are very much against that concept. We believe that the industry itself should be the judge. In representations before the committee there was agreement in principle on the need to facilitate and promote but a real question about the buy and sell provisions.
Let me draw a comparison with another industry that has not really been debated in the House. I know my time is almost up but I would like to look at the fishing industry. We all know about the Kirby Report. The fishing industry recently confronted the question of whether there should be significant government participation or intervention. The Kirby task force recently examined this question. The federal Government pushed for the creation of a Crown corporation, presumably one similar to Canagrex. However, the majority of participants in the fishing industry opposed such extensive government participation. They realized that they were better off keeping the Government out of their business operations wherever possible.
In its final report, the task force recommended the creation of an Atlantic Fisheries Marketing Commission to promote and co-ordinate market development with "minimum government involvement". This was a sound recommendation. It would have enabled the Government to facilitate marketing and exporting without being an active trader in the market. We, the Opposition, could accept a comparable role for
June 13, 1983

Canagrex. But Government members want a greater role in the agricultural industry, a greater role, ironically, than was created in the fishing industry. As a result, they have reserved judgment on the task force recommendation for a commission in the fishing industry. Indications are that they are unsatisfied with the amount of government control such a commission would provide and would only accept the commission if they saw it as a starting point from which they could eventually establish a full-fledged Crown corporation to meddle in the fishing industry. So far the fishing industry has resisted excessive government intervention in its sales management, and we must help the agricultural industry do the same. We can do that if we do not support the present Bill.
In my remaining two minutes there are two other matters upon which I would like to touch. They have been dealt with generally, as we have dealt with most of these issues, but I appreciate the chance to speak as I have not spoken on any stages of Bill C-85. There are other Hon. Members who were more involved in committee stage. I appreciate and respect that, but I also appreciate the chance to ventilate a few views today. There are two other flaws, in my humble opinion, in the Government's defence of Bill C-85. First, Hon. Members opposite assure us that Canagrex would be sufficiently accountable to Parliament and would not become yet another drain on the public purse. We are very apprehensive about that, regardless of the low initial budget and the best of intentions. I accept the best of intentions, but we only have to look at Canadair and some other Crown corporations to see that with low initial payments moneys have got out of control.
Second, the Government assures us that agricultural industry is largely in favour of Canagrex as it exists in Bill C-85. We do not accept that. Of the 32 groups that appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture to present their views on Canagrex, 20 were either opposed completely to the corporation or had reservations. These are some of the matters that I would like to discuss and that I find very unfortunate, but being in a very temperate spirit today, I will not even start talking about the club of closure which cuts me off at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a couple of questions for the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). He must be aware that the Government did not suggest Canagrex. Farm organizations suggested it. Also the Hon. Member referred to the fishing industry. Surely he is aware of the very successful Saltfish Corporation which has been in operation for several years. It is an ideal situation, as the Hon. Member will see if he wants to look at it and see how well it works. Is the Hon Member aware of the Saltfish Corporation?
Mr. Speaker, to answer both questions, I am most aware of the Saltfish Corporation. I was here when the matter was debated.

So was I.
Canagrex

Mr. Kirby looked at the total fishing industry. The recommendations are there. The fact of the matter is that we have an interesting paradox between what the Government is doing with Canagrex by creating a Crown corporation and the fishing industry. I am not talking about all the things which have been created. I am not making the case that there should not be Crown corporations in many areas. As the Minister stated in the debate, many Crown corporations are providing a good and fundamental service and are fulfilling a need which could not be fulfilled by the private sector.
In terms of agriculture, which is the most independent incentive-oriented individual industry in the country, our position is that we do not need the heavy hand of corporations to such an extent, which comes to the first question. Yes, I am aware, as the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) said earlier today in answer to a question from the Minister, that there was a concern and a need to have some type of assistance in export credits and export insurance and to facilitate marketing but, as the Minister well knows, no one from this side suggested we have the buy-and-sell or the joint venture.

Mr. Speaker, today we are continuing the debate on Bill C-58, to establish the Canagrex corporation. 1 would like to start by quoting Mr. William Jenkins, former dean of the Agricultural College of Nova Scotia, who said in an interview in 1981, and I quote:
In the Atlantic Provinces, exporting agricultural products is like a battle. It is every man for himself, a very primitive way of selling anything ... It is an almost chaotic state of affairs.
Canadian agriculture cannot afford this kind of situation, and that is why today, Mr. Speaker, we are considering the third reading stage of legislation to create a Crown corporation to be called Canagrex, and the purpose of this legislation is to provide for an effective mechanism that will help Canada find its true place on the international market for agri-food products. The corporation will be structured very carefully to provide for joint action by both public and private agents in the industry. It is not an attempt to take over the industry, as some Hon. Members have suggested or claimed. Canagrex will be a mechanism used by the industry in situations which historically have been obstacles to progress. It will provide financial, promotional and technical assistance and will also be used to facilitate identification of markets. Canagrex will be in a position to create markets, not to obstruct their development. Canagrex will therefore help Canada to provide, for the first time, a co-ordinated approach to its export markets. It will seek out new opportunities both for exporters that have been traditionally involved in the business and for newcomers to this field. In other words, Canagrex will make it possible for Canada to increase its profits on international export markets and to increase job opportunities within this country.

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
1 cannot believe that the Official Opposition could be against this concept. One of the most attractive aspects of this legislation is the fact that thanks to the new corporation, new exporters will be helped to get started in the business, and this will increase the variety of Canadian agri-food products available on export markets. Finally, Canagrex will be taking a very active interest in new exporters without harming those already in the business. It is clear that Canagrex will be acting only as a co-ordinating body when it meets requests for assistance from those engaged in the export business or those who intend to enter this field.
Canada's potential in the agri-food export field is unlimited but it has not been developed as well as it could be. We have the resources here in this country for truly taking advantage of our potential in an area which has often been thought of as too hard to "crack". We must know where our real potential lies. From there on, we can set our objectives and concentrate our efforts in order to attain a level of competitiveness that will be hard to beat. That is why I am surprised when I hear people say that the Government is trying to compete with the private sector in the agri-food industry. Nothing could be further from the truth, and to anyone who is still not convinced, I would suggest they read the legislation very carefully and they will realize that this is not the Government's intention. On the contrary, Canagrex will be able to help the farm export industry. We are not trying to take contracts away from the private sector. We want to make it possible for the private sector to grow and continue to play the important part it has played for so many years in the development of our export markets.
I can hardly accept the motion that some people are opposed to the establishment of Canagrex because they fear that the corporation might get involved in the purchase, sale or processing of farm products. The bill limits the use of these powers. Canagrex could be party to a contract only at the request of or in co-operation with a private concern, or if foreign countries showed interest in dealing only on a country-to-country basis. In this connection, please refer to Section 14(5) which states that Canagrex shall not engage in the export of farm products from Canada to other countries except in joint ventures or when acting on behalf of Canada as an agent of the Crown under country-to-country basis agreements.
Moreover, I repeat that most of the 11 members of the Board of directors will come from the private sector. Also, there will be an advisory committee, made up entirely of private sector representatives, which will provide advice and direction with a view to ensuring that Canagrex operates well.
The corporation will function on a three-year plan, which will serve as a basis for its operations and budget. At the end of a five-year trial period, a complete review of its operations will be carried out by the Standing Committee on Agriculture. As the Minister of Agriculture indicated in his remarks, Canagrex will be subjected to a yearly control by the Auditor General, which means that an integrated and complete audit
of all its operations will be carried out, something no other Crown corporation is required to have.
I should like to comment briefly on the importance of agrifood products in the context of our foreign trade. Last year, Canada's farm exports totalled $9.6 billion and its market surplus amounted to some $3.1 billion. Nearly 60 per cent of these products were made up of grain and oil seeds. Yet, if we compare the rest of our exports with our total exports, we find a non-grain deficit of some $2 billion. Canada has the resource potential to do much better than that and requires an agency similar to the Canadian Wheat Board to promote the sale of its non-grain products for export.
To increase our agri-food production, we need to develop new markets, and Canagrex could and should play an important role in this regard. We need this co-ordinating entity to ensure the development of our agri-food industry. Canagrex has no intention whatsoever of monopolizing any farm export. It can only use its powers in conjunction with the private sector to promote the export of agricultural products.
I cannot understand how behind the establishment of Canagrex some people can imagine a huge conspiracy to take over or harm the private sector. It is but a myth spread by a minority both inside and outside the private sector and I should like to take this opportunity to urge private enterprise to try to understand the predicament some very specialized producers find themselves in, since they get no assistance and lack the necessary mechanism to export their goods to foreign countries, for the benefit of Canada as a whole.
I would like to quote once again the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which many have already mentioned. I simply want to remind the Members that last November, during a meeting when it submitted a brief to us, the Federation said that Canada needed an export or agri-food products export assistance agency such as Canagrex that the government wants to create. The Federation also said that this legislation was aimed at producers. All producers are entitled to play a role in the agricultural export trade. By denying them this opportunity, we would be going against democratic principles.
Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the interventions made by Government Members on this side of the House and Members opposite. I have a great deal of respect for the opinions which have been expressed, but it seems to me that, especially in the agri-food sector, the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission have only played a very positive and creative role for Canada. Since their establishment, these two Canadian Government institutions have been the major innovators in agri-food production. They have been at the source of agricultural development in Canada. It saddens me that the opposition can imagine or fear that Canagrex could act against both farm producers themselves
June 13, 1983

and private companies which are already very successful in this field. I also want to say that the private sector greatly benefits from the international contacts which have been made and will continue to be made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). In this regard, I shall simply mention his visit to China and Mexico, where new markets were opened for all Canadian farm producers and the private sector, used them very successfully, for which I congratulate it.
In the future, if the Government as such or the Minister of Agriculture acting as an intermediary or Canagrex in its capacity as export development agent can enable the private sector and each farm producer in Canada to be better off, it will be to the advantage of everyone of us.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I would like, as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, to thank the Members of the Committee on the three sides of the table, if I may put it in these terms. During four months, we discussed this bill with a lot of interest and sometimes with passion, because each of us was very much concerned about what we wanted to see included in this legislation in order to meet as much as possible the needs and interests of agriculture producers. I would also like to thank all the witnesses who expressed their views to the committee. I would like to extend special thanks to the critic from the Official Opposition, the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), who was most helpful since this was my first experience in hearing witnesses on such an important bill. And I thank the representatives of the Official Opposition and of the New Democratic Party who were most effective and who led the discussion in a very positive and constructive way.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to express the hope that this day, June 13, will not be remembered by Canadians only as a sad day, because we have lost a Member of the Senate who has been a Member of this House and who was my neighbour for many years, namely Senator Maurice Lamon-tagne. Rimouski is only 20 miles away from Mont-Joli, and many Members of his family still live in the Lower St. Lawrence area, particularly in Rimouski. I would like this day to be also remembered as an auspicious day by agricultural producers in Canada. I trust that both the legislation and the regulations which will go along with it will make sure the Canagrex Corporation will be helpful to the agricultural community and will contribute to the wealth of Canada in our international trade.

Mr. Speaker, today is the third reading of Bill C-85, and a vote will be forced at 5.45 to terminate debate. Today may or may not turn out to be a good day for agriculture depending on how Canagrex performs. I do not undertsand why the Government is so reluctant to listen to the legitimate concerns that we in the Opposition are expressing on behalf of constituents who send us here to represent their views.
Canagrex
I would like to make two points, Mr. Speaker, in the ten minutes that I have in which to talk about Bill C-85, Canagrex. I would first like to touch on what the Government has been doing to help agriculture. It seems to me to be a sad commentary on the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) when he holds Canagrex out as being something that will help the industry when the industry is in considerable trouble and there are many other things that the Government could be doing to help agriculture. New legislation for the the Farm Credit Corporation was passed that included provisions for the agri-bond concept. We have seen nothing of that. In fact, I now hear that the Farm Credit Corporation is becoming very short of funds. A year ago in June of 1982, I heard the Minister say on an open line program in Winnipeg that the Farm Credit Corporation would very shortly have a large sum of money at preferred interest rates because of the Bill that had already been passed. We have not seen any of that.
As well, the Minister has done nothing for stabilization of the red meat industry. The first time that I ever visited Ottawa, this very beautiful capital of Canada, was in 1977 as a representative of the beef industry in Manitoba. At that time, I had the pleasure and privilege of appearing before a Senate committee that was looking into the beef industry. One of the recommendations that came out of that inquiry was that there be a stabilization program. For several years now, the industry has recommended that there be a stabilization program funded by the two levels of Government as well as the producers. The Minister has done nothing about that to assist the industry.
At the Liberal Party meeting which I believe was held in July, 1980, a resolution was passed to the effect that the Government should do something about capital gains. Again, the Government has done nothing about that. The reason I am making these points, Mr. Speaker, is to show that if the Government really wants to assist Canadian farmers and producers to export, it should be doing everything it can to make them competitive at home and to keep their cost down. After all, if we can produce a quality product with a competitive price, we will sell goods abroad. We will not be competitive on the international market if we cannot handle our costs and see that we produce effectively and efficiently at home.
One of the areas that we do have an advantage in is the area of energy. Yet look at what the Government has done to energy. It takes a great, big mark-up on every gallon of gasoline that goes into a farm tractor. That is one of the things that we on this side of the House have talked about for a long time. We want to cut down on the amount of tax taken by the federal Government when farmers burn fuel for the production of food. Yet no action has been taken on that.
It seems to me that if the Minister were really interested in doing something on behalf of the Canadian producer and farmer, he would be interested in talking to the farmer and working with the Provinces. We know that many of the Provinces are not in favour of the provisions of this Bill, particularly the buy and sell provisions of this Bill. We all agree with the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
June 13, 1983
Canagrex
Nystrom) who said that we need to support Canadian agriculture. There is absolutely no question about that.
We have a right to expect support back from the Government, and when I say we, 1 speak as a farmer. Look at the amount of taxation the Government takes from each farmer or from each acre of land that is farmed each year. It is an astronomical amount of money. To expect that the Government should put some of that money back is not expecting a lot.
I do not have time to go through the powers in Clause 14 of the Bill, but I am sure that every power conceivable was put into that Clause to make sure that the Government, through Canagrex, had as much access to power to purchase as possible. That concerns us. It is the same old story. When a farmer sees someone driving into his yard and that person says, "I am a Government man and I am here to help you", the farmer immediately becomes a little bit suspicious. We all know that farmers work very hard and that they are held accountable to their bankers. They have commitments to meet each year. When it is a Government operation, it is a little different. When somebody else's money is at risk, one does not get quite as involved. It is the same old story. Unless one risks one's own life or money, it is very easy to go through the whole process without becoming directly involved.
That is what concerns us about the buy and sell provision in the Bill. The Minister is kidding himself if he thinks those powers will not be used. If he is putting the powers in there and saying not to worry because they will not be used, that is fine, but if he is sincere, he should be prepared to take the powers away if they are not going to be used.
We can talk about what went on with PetroCan, for instance. It was supposed to be a small operation with a window on the industry to check things out. Now it is exploring for oil using Government dollars and it is checking oil and cleaning windshields. That is not what I understood to be the concept for PetroCan.
The Minister says we have to see what we can do about a $2 billion trade deficit in agricultural products in the country. I agree. We buy a tremendous amount of fruits and vegetables out of season because we cannot grow pineapples and oranges here. Canagrex is not going to achieve a lot in those areas.
I do not think the Minister is listening, Mr. Speaker. He likes to talk a lot but he does not listen very well. We can make sure that Canadian farmers are competitive. The Minister says that with Canagrex it will not be a case of the Government competing against farmers. That may be true, but what concerns me is that there are other programs in place and we do not want to see the Government competing against itself.
I have here the outline of a program in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce called the Program for Export Market Development for Food. The application form is quite extensive and applies to many areas that Canagrex will serve. How do we know that when Canagrex becomes operational there will not be a Canagrex Crown corporation competing with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce for a
share of export markets. With Government competing against Government and the first job of the bureaucracy being to grow, we know that our tax dollars are being used unwisely.
We have a legitimate concern about the proliferation of Crown corporations and the fact that they are not accountable. There may be all kinds of auditing after the fact but in many cases it is too late. We want to make sure that there is accountability up front. It seems to me that encouraging the private sector is the only way to get accountability up front.
The Minister is trying to ram the Bill through, and that is dividing the agricultural constituency, Mr. Speaker. Regardless of whether or not he believes it, we have very real concerns about the fact that the Government is becoming involved in joint ventures and in the actual production of food. Whether or not the Minister wants to admit it, that is the perception of the Bill.
I plead with the Government to remove the buy and sell provision and pass those parts of the Bill that everyone favours. That would be doing a service to agriculture and would enable us to show faith in the Government. It is not too late. I think everyone on this side of the House would agree with taking the buy and sell provision out of the Bill and leaving the good parts in there.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a brief moment to thank my colleagues for filling in and speaking on my behalf on my amendment to the Canagrex Bill, last week. I am glad to see that the Minister of Agriculture is in the House. I must say that I am very disappointed that Motion No. 2 standing in my name has been considered inappropriate and has been disallowed. I am genuinely concerned about that.
My remarks will deal almost exclusively with the implications that flow from this Bill for the beef cattle industry in Canada. I have spent a lifetime in that industry and have concerns that I want to put on the record.
I was disappointed that there was no proper debate on my motion. I understand it was disallowed on a rather trivial technicality. The motion was made in response to what I would describe as almost total support in the beef cattle industry. This was expressed very forcibly in the standing committee by a significant number of associations. The motion would have removed beef cattle and beef products from the legislation entirely. It was as simple and straightforward as that. It seemed it was disallowed because it was included in the interpretation section with two other exclusions already there, namely, fish and forestry products. That seemed the natural place to put it. I have since wondered if it would have suffered the same fate had it been included with two other exclusions in the Bill, dairy products and grain products, in Clause 14(2)(c)(i)(ii) in Bill C-85. I think it is fair to suggest that.
My main argument must be based on what I think is a very clear precedent that I found in the debate on Bill C-176 that took place 12 or 13 years ago. The Minister must have been here then; I was not but I was involved in the public debate at
June 13, 1983

that time in western Canada. That was the marketing board debate which went on for over two years, 1971 and 1972. At that time a similar amendment was proposed, debated and voted upon. The intent of that amendment was to exclude cattle and calves from the provisions of the Bill. A debate went on for many hours and included at least one all-night session. The important precedent is that this similar amendment was properly debated and the debate is recorded in Hansard.
My motion to amend Bill C-85 should have enjoyed the same right of debate in this House. After all, Acting Speaker Corbin ruled on July 29, 1982, as recorded at page 19829 of Hansard, that 1 might be able to present certain arguments in support of the acceptability of my motion.

speechtext: Order, please. The Chair has a certain difficulty at this point. The amendment was proposed by the Hon. Member and it was carefully considered by the Chair. The reasons for rejection of the amendment were offered. While I understand how the Hon. Member feels, he cannot reflect on that decision of the Chair.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In any event, 1 always felt that I personally, although perhaps informally, represented the total Canadian beef cattle industry in these matters and many others as well. I remind the House that almost all the organized beef cattle associations in Canada are vigorously opposed to Canagrex, especially to Article 14 of that piece of legislation, the powers to buy and sell. I make this statement on behalf of the following cattle organizations, all of which supported my amendment and so stated when they appeared before the committee meeting on Bill C-85. They are the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, the Alberta Cattle Commission, the Western Stock Growers Association, the Saskatchewan Stock Growers Association, and a number of other agricultural groups. Before leaving my references to the debate on Bill C-176, the marketing board legislation, I suggest that we could take another look at that debate, which took place many years ago, and consider the possibility of using the referendum or plebiscite approach which finally emerged out of that prolonged debate, which was also very emotional. It provided a way of resolving the difficulties in that earlier legislation. At least in western Canada agricultural producers were required to pass a majority referendum in each Province before such a proposal could be proceeded with. That was a preliminary step before a national board could be proceeded with. That pretty well resolved the difficulties. With only one or two exceptions, no marketing boards have been able to live with that criterion and successfully promote a national marketing board, certainly not in the cattle industry in Canada.
I would like to make a comment about the Canada All Breeds Association. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has made several references to this. This is a group of enterprising private enterprisers who are centered in Calgary. The managing director is Mr. Tony Saretsky. The Minister
Canagrex
knows this gentleman. The Minister has made several comments about this group and I am curious as to what his purpose is because here is a group which had a very tough time getting its organization operating, in the export of livestock particularly. It is finally now operating very successfully. Of course it has the power to buy and sell because it is a private enterprise outfit. It does operate with powers to buy and sell and it must have them.
This group appeared before our Standing Committee, and was totally opposed to Canagrex as we are now debating it. It seems to me that the Minister tends to forget this. This group was not out there promoting Canagrex. It was totally opposed to it. I believe the remarks of the Minister suggest that there is something wrong with the private sector having the powers to buy and sell. However, by the same token, he is arguing that because it does, his Canagrex legislation should indeed be entitled to the same powers. All I can say is, no way. This is not an argument which can be used to support the Government in requiring buy and sell powers. That is where private enterprise should be involved.
I would like to report briefly on the situation in our own Province of Alberta. This information was given to me very recently. It is from the office of our Minister of Agriculture in Alberta. The Alberta provincial Government is adamantly opposed to Canagrex because of the bad experiences it has had with its own Alberta export agency, and it has such an agency. It has had many cases ending up in court over this legislation and Alberta feels that the Government should not be allowed to be involved in marketing, referring to its own provincial Government, of course. This provincial legislation was in place for about four years during which there were nothing but problems. The same Alberta legislation, if it still exists at all, has not been used for over the last six years. This must surely be a clear indication that Alberta will very likely remove that legislation from its own books.
I would also like to make a comment about the remarks which have occasionally come from the Minister and others suggesting that, because the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is supportive of this Bill, some way or other it speaks for all other sectors of Canadian agriculture. I suggest very vigorously, Mr Speaker, that this is not necessarily so. The CFA does not, and never has, spoken officially for Canada's organized beef cattle producers. The Canadian cattlemen's associations, the Alberta Cattle Commission, the Western Stock Growers Association and the Saskatchewan Stock Growers Association, have never been members or affiliated with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The Minister should not leave the impression that the CFA is officially speaking for organized cattlemen in Canada. I object very strenuously to that impression.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to read a telegram which I received just the other day from the Saskatchewan Stock Growers Association. It is addressed to me. It reads:
During the Saskatchewan Stock Growers Association 70th annual convention held June 5th, 6th and 7th, the S.S.G.A. membership passed the resolution unanimously requesting that the federal Government withdraw cattle and cattle products from Canagrex. Again we state that Canagrex is redundant and duplicative of established programs. The private sector in conjunction with Industry, Trade and Commerce, has an excellent export performance and will not be improved by the intrusion of a new public agency. We wish to remind the Government that an overwhelming majority of western farm organizations oppose Canagrex. If there is a need for support to implement this legislation in certain sectors, the S.S.G.A. and all livestock groups wish to have their products excluded.
It then lists the various organizations, mostly in Saskatchewan but some in Manitoba, in that same telegram.
I would like to suggest that the Minister's laboured and selfconscious defence of the Government's use of closure, or time allocation, whatever you call it, is rather unimpressive. It does not matter what it is called, whether time allocation or closure, it is a spurious argument by the Minister that in no way changes the fact that the Minister, through his Bill, reduced the Canagrex debate to only two days for report stage and third reading. This same Minister was the hatchet man in the Crow debate at second reading to limit that debate to only one more day. These two pieces of legislation have upset, angered and totally frustrated all of western Canadian agriculture to an extent we have not seen since that marketing board legislation of about 13 years ago.
Canagrex is a nothing Bill which should never have come before Parliament in this form. There are presently under way in western Canada, especially in Alberta, public protest meetings going on regularly, and we have not seen this situation before, where they are protesting in the middle of their farming season to a very serious degree. I would like to close by saying that I will not be supporting this piece of legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
