Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this third reading debate on Bill C-85. Right at the start I want to place on the record that on second reading this Bill was debated for five days. It was considered in committee, witnesses were heard and amendments were discussed, for a total of 28 days, or 56 hours and 45 minutes. There were two days of debate at report stage, and now we come to the time when we will be voting on third reading and bringing this debate to a conclusion.
1 am one of those Canadian farmers who is not at all satisfied with our export market development over the years I have been farming. I was very upset that we have been expected to produce a product with no assurances as to price or quantity required for the export or domestic markets. By contrast, when I look at a June 9 article in The Globe and Mail I see that
China has ordered wheat from the Canadian Board valued at over $400 million. The article says:
The sale is part of a long term agreement with China that calls for the sale of between 3.5 million tons and 4.2 million tons annually for three years beginning in August, 1982.
What we have in the Canagrex legislation is something which will allow other sectors of the farm economy the opportunity to make long-term arrangements with the purchasing country, thereby assuring them continuity of supply of a quality product. I would like to quote from a letter of Mr. Gordon Hill, the Former Chairman of the Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board to the Editor of The London Free Press. I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that in 1950 and 1951 I was a committee man on that marketing board. Mr. Hill says:
The Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board was established in 1944. In 1967, by a vote of bean producers, agency marketing came into existence. The Marketing Board has grown in an orderly fashion since its inception and the dealer facilities have also expanded. This growth has resulted in a steady expansion of export business to the point that we currently average about 80 per cent of our $50 million worth of primary sales going into the export market. The beans are currently going to 28 countries around the world with an additional 25 countries participating in food aid.
He goes on to say:
The Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board feels that with the implementation of Canagrex, additional opportunities for trade will evolve from state-to-state trading, and the identification of new markets.
Canada is recognized, around the world, as a trading nation. Canagrex through its mandate can further develop this position.
Canagrex will be a winner for Canadian agriculture because its formation is a result of requests from grass root agriculturalists-the farmers.
Mr. Speaker, it is very clear that this Bill does have the support of farmers in eastern Canada, contrary to what others have said here today. The President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture stressed that "the powers which would be granted to Canagrex are not extraordinary. Rather than imposing a threat to free enterprise, it would be most beneficial to smaller agricultural producer groups which normally would not be able to crack the export market". He said Canagrex is absolutely essential if we are to fill the gaping void between our potential to produce and manufacture agricultural products for export and our present performance.
Just last week, Mr. Speaker, I had inquiries from two small processing companies requesting assistance in filling export contracts. Together with them I contacted the various Government Departments and agencies. The word came back to us that as of that date there were no programs available for these two small companies, but the departmental people told me that if Canagrex were in place, that body could facilitate their needs.
There are a lot of areas I would like to touch on in this debate, but there seems to be a perception that Canagrex is going to get involved in primary food production. That is not the case. One of the amendments to Clause 14 in committee was that if Canagrex aquires property for lease or otherwise, it does not include the power to purchase, lease or otherwise acquire real property for the production of fruit, forage, grain,
June 13, 1983

vegetable or other crops, and so on. Canagrex cannot get involved in actual production for domestic or export, unless it is in coordination with or at the request of other groups who wish the assistance of Canagrex, it cannot get involved in production except for new market development.
The make-up of the board of directors of Canagrex is clearly spelled out in the legislation. Seven of those directors have to come from outside the civil service. But there will be one from each of the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Finance from within the Civil Service. I would hope we would have some expertise from the red meat sector. The Canadian Pork Council supports Canagrex, and I would expect they would want to be involved because they are very aggressively going after export markets. I would also hope there will be one from the poultry sector because they are very forward looking as far as export markets are concerned. Perhaps Canagrex will be the missing link we have been looking for to enable us to plan our poultry and livestock production and know that we have continuity of supply for the countries which wish to import the food. Certainly I would hope the horticultural sector would have someone involved in this agency as well. Naturally, we need some business and trading expertise too. I would hope we would have a blend of expertise, people who will work together on the production of food so amply produced here in Canada to supply world markets. 1 believe there is tremendous opportunity here for Canadians.
I see the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) has just come into the House. 1 have had inquiries from the Tobacco Marketing Board about the progress of the Canagrex legislation and the need for it in that particular industry. I have tobacco producers in my own riding who are vitally concerned about the fact that more and more countries want to deal on a state-to-state basis. They envisage new markets opening up because Canada has the highest quality tobacco of any country in the world. It is only human nature for the farmer to want to expand his production to supply those markets.
The legislation before us today, Mr. Speaker, was started quite a few years ago, first of all through a series of meetings of the major farm organizations in Canada with input from the various sectors. They discussed the concept, the needs, and they saw the shortfall of the organizations already in place. They felt that, with the high cost of production in Canada, we had to have some vehicle to act as a focal point to bring together not only the production sector but the processors, packers and exporters to work together in a meaningful partnership on behalf of the whole Canadian economy. It is very interesting that in some of those early meetings the Canadian Labour Congress was involved. They followed the development of this legislation in the discussion stage. They saw the spin-off effects, what it would do for job creation. They recognized that this is a good piece of legislation and we had to proceed if we were to realize our potential. The Canagrex formula, guided by the philosophy of serving the needs of all the producers to facilitate the agri-food industry, would assist in the diversification of products offered to the foreign buyer.
Canagrex
The potential market possibilities are real. Conditions in the marketplace indicate that with a co-ordinated approach Canadian agri-food exports could stand on a firmer footing and become a more potent competitor. I recently had inquiries from two different countries which wanted to import Canadian dairy cattle, the Canadian Holstein-Friesian. That breed is one of the most efficient producers of dairy products in the world. There are two countries that want to import that cattle, but they will need the help of Canagrex to fulfil that mandate.
One can see the fragmented approach which is taken by the various Provinces. I understand that the Province of Quebec presently provides a subsidy of $250 for each animal going into the export field. How do other Provinces compete against that? Consequently, we need a co-ordinating body such as Canagrex to fulfil that need to ensure that the product is available for those markets and the back-up services are provided so that the animals are put on the correct rations and kept in the proper environment to produce to their capacity.
I think it is only fair to look at Canagrex in the context of the missing link between our marketing board structures which are already in place in Canada. That structure did not recognize the potential which we had in Canada. The marketing boards themselves should be a body which is expansionary in concept in terms of striving to fill those markets whether they are in Canada or outside. Canagrex can be the mechanism to utilize that potential.
The former chairman of the White Bean Growers Marketing Board wrote a letter to the editor in which he recognized the need for the various other marketing boards which we have. I hope Canagrex will be able to work very closely with these organizations and provide the bridge financing required when necessary, which may include terms for payment six months down the road.
Possible market potential as identified by Agriculture Canada and other federal Government agencies relates directly to the need for Canada to begin to be more dynamic in export marketing. This is not a condemnation of what has traditionally taken place in the agri-food sector but rather a recognition of the ever changing world of the export marketplace. It is an ever changing world that shows that there is a quiet and subtle trade war evolving between the United States and the European Common Market. This is happening more often and the competition is becoming stronger. Can those other two countries, without the marketing board structures such as we have in Canada, assure themselves of long-term continuity of supply of a quality product or will they have to rely on programs such as the PIK Program which is in place in the United States? Do we know what these markets will be next fall? Do we know what crops will be in Russia? Do we know what they will be in the United States, let alone Ontario?
Since export markets are traditionally highly volatile, the best way for Canada to achieve additional exports in nongrains is also to create a strong and stable domestic market for

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
those commodities. This will help meet the objective of reducing the trade deficit in certain sectors of the non-grains area as Canagrex will help industry in linking export development and import replacement. I cannot help but reflect on the 1982 statistics which show that the dollar value of wheat sales last year was up by 15 per cent over 1981 while export sales in other sectors of the agricultural industry are up by only 2 per cent. Surely we must have a more efficient system than the one that exists at the present time.
I am reminded of a book entitled "Not for Export" which was written by a Carleton University professor. Ele points out many of the problems with which we are confronted today. These problems date back to the 1800s, to the time of Confederation. He points out the fact that all too often we have subsidiary companies in Canada whose head offices are located elsewhere. Consequently, when an order is placed it is not filled by the Canadian subsidiary but by the parent company in another country. Canagrex can give us a clear Canadian identity and also ensure that we have the mechanisms in place by which the Government can work with producers to fill those markets if requested to do so.
While Canada does have a number of export market tools at present, as a country we have not moved to present to the foreign buyer an agri-food focus for exports. Our efforts are fragmented and this tends to lead to what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture referred to as missed opportunities.
Similarly, potential exports of Canadian agricultural products have suffered because they have not had the means to become involved in world trading. Canagrex can be the catalyst by which doors of opportunity will open through various programs as outlined in the legislation for these potential exporters.
The benefits to the Canadian agri-food industry both in the long and short term will be significant because it will enable Canada to offer a more diversified range of product possibilities to foreign buyers. This can be of benefit to the industry and to the country's over-all balance of trade.
What all this points to is that Canagrex will, over the long run, have an opportunity to develop a trade philosophy which will relate directly to increased foreign trade dollars for Canada and the creation of additional employment. Whether that employment is in the agricultural industry itself or a related industry, there must be a concentrated effort to ensure that we get our share of these foreign markets. These spin-off effects will be felt throughout the Canadian economy.
I urge passage of this important legislation. The markets are out there and Canada can and will be competitive in all areas to ensure that we capture those markets as identified by Agriculture Canada and other Government agencies. I believe that it will take three years before we are able to bring our true trade potential into focus. I hope that Members of the Opposition will work together with the Government to ensure that the farm organizations will have their views taken into consideration. For example, I hope that the red meat sector in Canada will be able to partake in the benefits of this legislation, whether it is only the participation of the Pork Council at the present time or the ability to become competitive in the near
future as far as the marketing of beef in offshore markets is concerned.
When I look at the trade figures in Hong Kong and see one of our major Canadian exporters getting one-third of his trade from another country to fill that market, I would hope that Canagrex would become very actively involved there to fill that market with Canadian products. The spin-off effects would benefit our total economy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, if there is anything pleasant to say about this Bill, it is simply to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for staying at least once in the House during debate on a piece of legislation related to agriculture. It is nice to have "Green Gene" in the House when we are debating subject matter of this nature.
It is an insult to this Parliament, the people of Canada and the farming community of the country that with a Bill of this magnitude on which there is this diversity of opinion and which has poisoned and marinated the prospective discontent that is divided largely between East and West, the Minister would bring it to the House under the guillotine of closure. This piece of legislation does not strive toward achievement but strives toward power. This represents an attempt by the Government to achieve complete and absolute Government involvement in farm management in the farming communities of this country. That is the kind of extent of Government involvement with which we will end up in Canada where Government will control farm management.
As long as the Government controls the concept of marketing and its process, then in effect the Government controls all management decisions. The farmers, following the passage of this legislation, at least until that Party is on the Government side of the House, will find out that the right of control and decision-making has slid from the farm desk to the bureaucracies of the corporation called Canagrex. With respect to the buy and sell power, the Minister, very wrongly, told us today it is analagous to that which is used by Crown corporations in the Province of Alberta.
If I might, Mr. Speaker, I want to take just a moment to share with you the great illusion under which the Minister of Agriculture buries himself and to the way in which he deceives the people of Canada by simply mentioning those names.
In the Constitution of the Soviet Union we note there is freedom of speech, freedom of association and also people have freedom of travel. The only difference is that a person in the Soviet Union has to get a permit to go from Moscow to Kiev. While the Minister of Agriculture quite rightly says that in the Province of Alberta with its Crown corporations there are provisions for buy-sell, what he said is really like trying to make the analogy of a North American claiming he is free or a citizen of the Soviet Union claiming he is free. Both Constitutions say the words but the facts are not the same.
June 13, 1983

The Minister of Agriculture said today in his speech that the Province of Alberta has buy-sell power. 1 simply say to him that if he thinks those two buy-sell programs are the same, he deceives this House. The fact is that if the Government used the buy-sell provisions as defined by the Province of Alberta, it would find that they are far less offensive than the buy-sell definition in this Bill. Sure the words are the same in the title, but what is the actual legislation? There are four pages of definition in the description marked Canagrex. In the very first paragraph of Clause 14 it reads:
(a) purchase agricultural products and food products and package-
Package. Let me emphasize "and package."
-process, store, ship, insure, import, export or sell or otherwise dispose of products purchased by it;
To package or otherwise sell is the extent to which it will go. We could wind up in the supermarkets of the country and on the Canagrex shelf find Whelan beans. With the label reading "It's ours." We can get rid of all the various kinds of food labels we see on cans and replace them with "Canagrex. It's ours."
The Minister across the way tells us about something or another but his implications are that I am simply fabricating the facts. But we all recall the days in 1972 when the Liberal Minister of Energy was going around the country telling people "Don't fear PetroCan" because it is simply to be, and 1 quote from that period of time, "a window on that industry."
We were told that all the Government wanted was to get into the board rooms to see how the oil industry worked. The Minister of the day said we had no reason at all ever to be associated with the service station end of the industry. That window on the industry, PetroCan, became an employer of 8,000 people and it ended up right in marketing at street level. The point to be made is that once power is granted, power is used. If the Minister thinks I am fallacious in my imagination of the full extension of the use of the power as defined, then the Minister defies history. When you grant power, as I said the power ends up by being used.
I join with many others in opposing this legislation. I am in good hands in saying that I will vote against this Bill later this day. Noting that the last speaker for the Liberal side listed two or three groups saying they are in favour of the Canagrex legislation, let me put on the record the fact that the following are opposed to this legislation:
Alberta Beekeepers Association, Ablerta Canada All Breeds Association, Alberta Canola Growers Association, Alberta Cattle Commission, Alberta Pork Producers Marketing Board, British Columbia Cattlemen's Association, British Columbia Pork Producers Association, Canadian Cattlemen's Association, Canadian Export Association, Canadian Meat Council, Canadian Seed Trade Association, Consumers' Association of Canada, Flax Growers Western Canada, Manitoba Canola Growers Association, Manitoba Cattle Producers' Association, Ontario Bean Dealers Association, Palliser Wheat Growers Association, Saskatchewan Canola Growers Association, Saskatchewan Hog Marketing Commission, Saskatchewan Stockgrowers' Association, Shippers and Exporters Association, Western Barley Growers' Association, Western Stockgrowers' Association-
And the list goes on. This Minister operates in the milieu of deceit, Mr. Speaker, when he implies to us that there is some kind of blanket acceptance in general for his legislation. He
Canagrex
operates on the fact that by far the majority of Canadians are in favour of his legislation. I know there are people in the Province of Quebec and in the Province of Ontario, even to some extent in the Maritime Provinces, who believe this legislation would be good for them. We in this Party are willing to accept that that marketing agency is of some value. But it is absolutely unacceptable to have that legislation contain Clause 14 with such a full extension of power, with that vast number of associations, which 1 have listed, opposed to it, and for the Minister to come to the House and tell us that there is broad acceptance, when in fact there is not, and for the Minister to do this under the threat of closure. That defies the democratic process by which we come to represent our constituents. I tell you, Sir, this piece of legislation is, for that reason, unacceptable.
The time is all too short in this debate, particularly because of closure. I have an agreement with my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) to share some time. I want to wrap up by saying that this Minister of Agriculture who often gives himself praise, irre-gardless of the fact there is no such word as irregardless, and who keeps et cetering his way through the House, has never before passed a major piece of legislation in all the years he has been Minister of Agriculture. Today we will have his first piece of major legislation in all the years he has been the Minister. This will be done through closure. It has taken him three years. He has stubbornly done it without listening to any amendment. He has stubbornly done it without listening to the majority of the agricultural communities in Canada, and he will obtain this legislation only because he prefers closure to democracy. I tell you, Sir, he is the worst Minister of Agriculture in the history of the country. I will now sit down so that I can share the speaking time with the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster who will take off on this Minister with equal tenacity. I hope he will call for his resignation.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) for allowing me to take part in this debate. It seems strange that we must now share the 20-minute speaking time allowed each Member because of the rush and the inability of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to convince the majority of Canadians that this Bill called Canagrex is needed. We have closure imposed upon us.
Time allocation.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Therefore, as Members we must share the time and limit our debate so that this legislation may be imposed against the will of the majority of the farming communities and producers in Canada.
I want to say a few words on the supposed need and the great benefit that will accrue from this Crown corporation to be imposed on the people of Canada. I guess that we should not be concerned. I guess it is the right of the Government to pass bad legislation. It has not stopped the Government in the past. I suppose it will not stop the Government in the next six

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
to ten months on whenever the Government screws up enough courage to call an election. The people of Canada will find a method of removing this bad legislation from the books. That is called a general election, and certainly we on this side of the House look forward to that opportunity.
The need for Canagrex, as expressed by the Minister and by other Government Members, is that it will increase the volume of goods which can be exported from Canada. Let us take a look at some of the things that have happened without this Crown corporation. I will be referring to ten-year averages from 1968 to 1970. For example, the export of buckwheat increased 94 per cent in ten years. Corn went up 12,000 per cent without any help, without any marketing agency imposed upon the growers against their will. Turning to flaxseed, it went up 14 per cent in ten years, and soyabean went up 149 per cent. Now let us talk about the Cinderella crop of western Canada, canola, which was originally rapeseed. It increased 258 per cent without a Government marketing agency or without a Crown corporation to sell it. I think the numbers and the commodities speak for themselves. The exporters of these goods, the people who work along with the producers of these commodities to export them into the world, are doing a very good job.
There is an opportunity for the Government to become involved. The Government has had that opportunity for the past number of years with Government agencies to which it could have given assistance. Let us look at the new crops, the pulse crops which are coming on board in western Canada. They are being marketed by individual enterprisers without a Crown corporation. Canary seed and lentils, pulse crops in my part of Canada, are taking a large amount of acreage and are providing producers with a beneficial return. The only reason they grow these crops is that they make a profit. Exporters are making a profit and are encouraging it. I think they are doing it very well.
During the short time allowed in the House for this debate we continually heard the Canadian Wheat Board being compared with Canagrex. Anyone who knows anything about the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board and its structure compared with Canagrex would be amazed that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) or the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Dionne) would have the audacity to compare them. The Canadian Wheat Board is funded by producers. It is operated out of the hip pockets of farmers. Also it has an elected advisory board. Free and democratic elections take place. They advise the Canadian Wheat Board. There are five commissioners appointed by the Government of Canada. No one, not even the strongest critics of the Canadian Wheat Board, could say that any of the five commissioners were painted with a political brush of one stripe or another. The producers of western Canada fund the Canadian Wheat Board out of their sales. They feel they have control over that Board. They do not have a worry about it because it is funded out of their pockets. They provide the operating
money. They are the ones who have input through their elected advisory board.
When we take a look at the review by the Auditor General in the Bill, we realize that it comes three years after it has started. I cannot understand why a review would be allowed only after three years. Why could it not be allowed after the first or the second year? It is far too late.
The Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) presented an amendment which in my opinion was certainly a reasoned and rational one. When we consider that wheat and dairy products are excluded and that by far the vast majority of cattle associations in the country were against their product being included in the Bill to establish Canagrex, why would the Minister not listen to cattlemen as well as he listened to wheat growers and dairy producers? I think this is unbecoming of a Minister of Agriculture who is a democrat and has the best interests of agriculture at heart. There is some difficulty at times recognizing that, but I do not understand why he would not listen to the loud voice of cattle producers and breed associations of Canada. They did not ask for the Bill to be killed or for it to be removed from the Order Paper; they only asked that their product not be included.
When we take a look at the Bill, we find that it is redundant, inappropriate and misdirected. Presently the Government has at its disposal all the means it needs to support export growth in agriculture. With only a few minor enlargements of the mandate of the Export Development Corporation, the Canadian Commercial Corporation and the Foreign Trade Service, they could quite adequately fulfil the financing and marketing needed to support exports. I think that could be done at a much lower cost to Canadian taxpayers.
It is mot inappropriate that through Canagrex the Government could establish itself as a direct trader with the power to buy and sell on international markets. As we have indicated previously, it will bring unfair competition to bear on the existing export structure. The consequences of the unfair competition will have a negative effect on over-all trade performance in the export field. It is misdirected because the basic issue in Canada's export growth has been totally ignored by Canagrex. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) identified the crucial issue, that is our ability to supply internationally competitive prices. The Government proposal for Canagrex does not address that problem.
We have had discussions about international trading organizations in the House. We had a special standing committee of the House of Commons which travelled to gain knowledge as to whether an international trading corporation would be necessary and would be of assistance to the people of Canada. On June 28, 1982, I asked the then Minister of State for International Trade, the Hon. Member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley), why he was even considering supporting Canagrex when he, as Minister responsible, had not seen fit to go ahead with the implementation of an international trading corporation. If the international trading corporation for other products was not acceptable to the Government, why would it
June 13, 1983

find acceptable to impose upon the agricultural community the Bill before us?
During this debate we have heard Hon. Members on the Government side indicate that the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) was responsible for the Bill. Any time the discussion of Canagrex arose, as the Minister of Agriculture and his Parliamentary Secretary should know full well, the Hon. Member for Elgin did not at any time endorse the buy and sell proposal. Under his direction it was to be a Bill to facilitate, assist and encourage, but at no time distract from the individual initiatives of exporters and producers.
After straightening out the record in that regard, I will sit down as my time has expired, but I will certainly rise in my place to vote against Bill C-85.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Kinders-ley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) stated that he finds it hard to understand why grains produced under the Canadian Wheat Board and dairy products which are sold under the Canadian Dairy Commission were being pulled out of the Bill. He cited that as an example or a reason why livestock production should be exempted from the Bill as well. Grain producers and dairy producers which have marketing organizations work with them. Therefore, I can understand that exemption.
Can the Hon. Member explain to the House how exempting livestock, something which did not pass in committee by the way, from the powers of the Bill would meet the requirements or expectations of his fellow Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) who in his speech on second reading was hoping that a Canagrex operation would assist some of his constituents to export calves to Israel. That is now possible with the way the Bill has been handled. What would he propose to do for his fellow Member for Provencher if livestock and beef cattle had been exempted from the Bill?

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I guess I should not be surprised at the question because it comes from the philosophy shared by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse). Number one, the dairy producers of Canada want a dairy marketing board, they have one and that is what they should have because they want it. Number two, the Canadian wheat producers want a Canadian Wheat Board, they have it and they should have it. Number three, Canadian cattlemen do not want a marketing board. They do not want Canagrex. If we can recognize those facts and those democratic responses of those who produce goods, then we will live in a democracy which continues to function. As to what I would do for my colleague from Provencher, I would explain to his constituents that there is already the Canadian Export Development Corporation and the Canadian Commercial Corporation which could facilitate and assist in financing the export of calves all over the world. We do not need Canagrex in order to export cattle.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Hon. Member. First, is he aware that in the Province of
Canagrex
Saskatchewan the provincial Minister of Agriculture, the Deputy Premier and House Leader for that Province, is using the Crown corporations set up by the previous Government to export cattle to Romania? It has the power to buy and sell. Is the Member also aware that he is not intending to abandon any Crown corporations in Saskatchewan at the present time because they are all making money? Is he aware of that?
Also, is he aware that it is not closure that is being used in the House of Commons? In the books of procedure there is a definition for closure and a definition for time allocation. The most democratic Parliament in the world, the Mother of Parliament in Great Britain, uses time allocation nearly every day that it is in session. Is he aware of that? Why does he continue to try to get across the point that this Minister of Agriculture, who has been elected for 37 years in the most democratic forms of Government that there is, would do anything that would be undemocratic?

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would never question the good judgment of the good people of the county which the Hon. Minister comes from, but I am sure that some of them have found 37 years a bit trying on their patience and look forward to an apportunity to change that.
In answer to the Minister's question, yes, I am aware that cattle is exported from Saskatchewan through the Saskatchewan Agricultural Corporation. That is because the people of Saskatchewan want that Crown corporation. The Minister of Agriculture finds that humorous.
I do.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: In Saskatchewan there happens to be a Government that recognizes the value of Crown corporation. If he looks at the restructuring of Crown corporations in Saskatchewan he will find that they have become fiscally responsible. Second, there has been the elimination of some Crown corporations since the return of the Progressive Conservative Government in Saskatchewan. Third, when the Minister refers to closure, anything that limits debate and stops the democratic process short of fulfilment is closure. When closure is administered in committee by the Liberal and NDP Members to stop the Saskatchewan stock growers and Saskatchewan honey producers from appearing before the Standing Committee on Agriculture and presenting their feelings and their case, it does not matter what it says in the Standing Orders, it is closure and a gagging of the democratic process.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Hon. Member. It seems that the main problem the Official Opposition has with Canagrex is the buy and sell power. Is he aware that a commercial corporation has existed since the 1940s and that it has exactly the same powers as Canagrex in commercial areas? With regard to certain agricultural commodities, this corporation has been doing exactly what Canagrex is proposed to do, and has been doing for a great many years with regard to canola, that is, the Canadian Commercial Corporation. It has been doing a very fine job. We had the Estimates before the Finance Committee not more than two

June 13, 1983
Canagrex
weeks ago. Members opposite were present. That corporation was given a glowing round of applause for the work that it has been doing. Indeed, Members asked why it had not moved into the agricultural area and whether it could do the kinds of things that Canagrex is proposed to do. Members of that committee were told that yes, it could, if the Government and the Opposition wanted it to do so, but Canagrex was being designed specifically to deal with agricultural commodities. That is why the Canadian Commercial Corporation is not moving into that area.
We have had a corporation like this for a great many years with the buy and sell power and with the power to deal state to state. It does not currently have the power to deal state to private sector, but it could have if the Government gave it that mandate. It could do that by simply saying, "Would you please do it". It would not even take a change in parliamentary legislation.
We have this corporation already. It has been doing a good job. It has been serving the farmers of western Canada with regard to canola very well. The Crown corporation does exist. If that is the case, why all this great hue and cry when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) brings forward legislation to provide an agricultural equivalent to the Canadian Commercial Corporation?

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response, I would pose a question to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). He must not be aware that under the Agriculture Products Act the Minister of Agriculture already has those powers. They are all there, they have been there for a long time and the Minister did not use them. He said he needs a new Act, a whole new Bill. He needed more powers when he had all the powers which the Member for Ottawa Centre asks for.
We have the Canadian Commercial Corporation which has powers in agricultural export also, and the Government did not use them. It wanted to bring in another Bill, a Canagrex Bill designed specifically for agriculture. When we look at other countries that have state-controlled agriculture and export organizations, we see that they are not doing so great when it comes to feeding their own people. We in Canada have been doing pretty well. That is one of the reasons why we are suspect. All these powers have been in these two Acts. We are not sure why the Minister wants to bring in more.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak in the House to a Bill we shall be adopting today, whose purpose is to create the Canagrex corporation. I think Canada has a duty to acquire this export mechanism if it is to remain competitive with other countries in the world that are taking concrete steps to extend export markets for their agricultural products. These countries, which are providing some very stiff competition, have already taken steps to increase their exports of agri-food products, and I am thinking
more particularly of our neighbours to the South, the Americans.
In fact, the U.S. has several mechanisms, such as the Foreign Agriculture Service, the Co-operative Program, the Commodity Credit Corporation and many related credit programs such as Public Law 480, which are aimed at improving their agri-food exports which are already earning $36 billion for the U.S.. This shows the kind of priority set by countries like the United States on exports of agri-foods products. Other countries have followed suit, including France, Denmark, Great Britain, Germany, Israel and Mexico, and set up appropriate mechanisms to maximize the development of their export markets.
The powers granted to agencies in the United States to facilitate sales of agricultural products provide for a sensible and flexible approach to seeking out export markets. It is also very interesting to note that the industry is seeking further powers. In addition, many groups are in favour of increased coordination of efforts, and pressure is very strong for adopting the Export Trading Act, which will create export trading companies similar to the Japanese giants that deal with all aspects of exports. In other words, Canada will be facing increasing competition on the market, and it must act now before it is too late.
Some people claim that Canagrex will not be like the mechanisms that already exist in other countries for the purpose of developing exports of agri-food products. Nothing could be further from the truth! Our competitors are not competing with other sectors in their own countries but with other countries. They have created agencies to facilitate sales to foreign buyers, in order to maximize sales of their products. That is exactly what Canagrex will do: Act as an agent to facilitate and promote, through all its members as enumerated in the Bill, the rapid sales of Canadian agri-food products on foreign markets.
Mr. Speaker, to illustrate what is now happening to the export of Canadian agri-food products in certain sectors, I would like to quote the comments made by Mr. William Jenkins, former dean of the Nova Scotia College of Agriculture, during an interview last year. He said:
In the Atlantic provinces, the export of farm products is like a war. It is every man for himself, which is a very rudimentary way of selling any product ... It is nearly perfect chaos.
The Canadian agricultural industry cannot afford this. What the other countries are now doing to prevent such a war only confirms the importance of Canadian competition on export markets. I therefore urge the House to give rapid passage to the Bill on Canagrex by voting for it this evening. Thanks to the markets it will provide abroad, this corporation will help our farmers as well as Canada as a whole.
I heard earlier some Progressive Conservative Members who seemed at one point to give the impression that everyone is against the establishment of Canagrex, but I would like to
June 13, 1983

mention a few organizations that have supported Bill C-85, such as the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, which stated that the Canagrex Bill should be passed during this session, and that the agricultural industry desperately needs such a legislation.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture also sent a brief to members on both sides of the House in which it expressed its serious concern about the Canagrex issue. The Federation believes that it is desirable that such a development corporation have all the flexibility required to promote the development of Canadian exports, to take the risk of joint ventures, to provide specialized advice if need be, to negotiate from state to state in many circumstances where it is desirable or essential to share the risks and support long-term development, meet publicity requirements, provide guarantees and allow its employees to accept responsibility if required and to actively seek market opportunities.
And to that end, Mr. Speaker, in a document recently made available to us, it was stated that in the maple syrup industry, in particular, it was expected that with the setting up of this Canagrex corporation, sales could be arranged right now or at least over the next few months, the next few years, for up to $5 or $6 million more on markets such as Germany or Japan. I feel this is most important, especially in my constituency of Levis, on the South Shore, where a number of maple syrup producers, especially in the Beauce, Bellechasse and Lotbiniere areas have been faced over these last few years with important surpluses. It is my view that Canagrex comes at the right time in these circumstances to allow those maple syrup producers to unload or sell on export markets that production that is so expensive in Canada and in Quebec. I therefore expect that our Progressive Conservative friends cannot afford to oppose that over a long period.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture goes on to say that in their view, they cannot but conclude that the opposition to Canagrex should not be considered as a valid or substantive opposition but rather as a concern that the Corporation might be mismanaged and misused, that it might further its own expansionist goals without regard to the commodity sectors involved.
In setting up Canagrex, we explicitly and specifically say that for once, from its very beginning, we will have a Crown corporation that will be submitted to the control of the Auditor General. Reference is made to integrated audit, to reports which will have to be submitted to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. And these will come back to the House. I think that we have all the possible safeguards to make sure that the corporation will be efficiently managed.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we had the opportunity to meet with spokesmen for the Union des producteurs agricoles who were heard several times in connection with grain transportation and I have in mind that well-known Gilson report. In this case as with the policy on grain transportation, the UPA is begging the government to pass this legislation on Canagrex. I refer to a statement made by the UPA spokesman who
Canagrex
appeared before the Senate committee on February 2, 1983 and I quote:
The UPA welcomes, therefore, the principle of creating a corporation intended to promote, improve and diversify our export of agricultural and food products, and supports entirely the position taken by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to that effect. We hope, nevertheless, that Quebec will be adequately represented within Canagrex and that this Corporation will show both flexibility and good judgment in using the powers which are given to it. Finally, we hope fervently that the Federal Government will provide to Canagrex all the necessary funds for its effective functioning and that, on the other hand, the work of Canagrex will never be hampered by the sloth and bureaucratic complexity which are too often found in this kind of corporation.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and all of us have done a good job and in this legislation we have all the provisions required by the UPA.
And the UPA representative added this, since the submission of this brief, the UPA in particularly its president, Mr. Jacques Proulx, has constantly reiterated its support for the creation of a corporation to promote the export of agricultural and food products, and to press for the passage of Bill C-85, as can be seen from the various telegrams of which copies are appended to today's brief and which were sent to the Minister of Agriculture, the Prime Minister of Canada, the government House Leader, the leader of the official opposition, various federal and provincial ministers and the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
Finally, last autumn, the UPA began to study the amended text of Bill C-85, as tabled by the Commons Standing Committee on Agriculture on July 19, 1982. After studying the amendments, the UPA declared itself to be completely in agreement with the proposed changes, while continuing to press for all the recommendations contained in its brief of April, 1982.
As well, Mr. Speaker, a spokesman for the Montreal Board of Trade appeared before the same Senate committee. I will quote him to indicate, as I said earlier, that someone may have been trying to give the impression that we are creating some kind of monster which will be a disservice to the agricultural community, but I think that by now we have the proof that many agricultural organizations support the establishment of Canagrex. Here is the statement which can be found in the minutes of the proceedings of the Senate Standing Committee on Agriculture of Tuesday, February 1, 1983:
What we need is some way of guaranteeing steady supply-multi-year contracts-and, in addition, assisting with infrastructure in the receiving country because many of the countries we are talking about do not have the sophistication in terms of infrastructure-
I think that the Montreal Board of Trade goes further than the other organizations. It even talks about giving immediate and direct assistance to those countries which might eventually become our clients.
The spokesman for the Montreal Board of Trade went on to
say:
One of the reasons Canagrex is needed is that we have to start developing longterm markets. We have to do that to, basically, find out that specific research we need in order to match our ability to produce and the product we produce to the markets. It seems to me that nobody is doing enough in terms of finding out what

Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act
the needs and plans are in each country and converting that to what Canada has. Although research is covered in the bill, it seems to me that this would have to be done in co-ordination. Canagrex would be only a catalyst to get the research done. I do not think Canagrex should be the researcher per se.
We, as a country, have to export more agricultural products. Agribusiness is one of only about five areas of Canada's industry and economy where we can actually grow and, in fact, create employment. Referring to information I received from the Financial Post conference, there is capacity in Canada to produce two-thirds again the amount of agricultural products we currently produce.
Mr. Speaker, I have also read in Le Devoir an article by Florent Plante. It said that the National Council of the Parti Quebecois was warning farmers against Bill C-85 concerning Canagrex. I have been sitting in this House for a little more than two years, and my experience tells me that when the Parti Quebecois says that a proposal by the federal government should be rejected, it means precisely that it is time to approve this proposal. I believe we had had many examples of this in the last couple of years or months.
Also, we had the opportunity during the weekend to witness the nomination of a new leader for our friends in the Progressive Conservative Party, and I suggest we should perhaps ask Mr. Mulroney what is the position of this party concerning the establishment of Canagrex.
I think the time has come to ask the real questions, now that the convention is over, now that all those nice things have been said. Perhaps the time has now come to ask the new leader-
